speechtext: That a special committee consisting of thirty members to be named later be appointed to study the several amendments to the Dominion Elections Act, 1938, and amendments thereto, suggested by the chief electoral officer, to study the said act, to suggest to the house such amendments as the committee may deem advisable, and report from time to time, with power to send for persons, papers and records and to print the proceedings, and that the provisions of section 1 of standing order 65 be waived in respect to this committee.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND SUGGEST AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we were not informed at six o'clock yesterday that this notice of motion would be proceeded with today. I had a few words that 1 wanted to say about it, and since the motion has now been called perhaps I have no alternative but to express at this time my thoughts on the motion.
I am sure we are all in agreement with the practice that is followed of setting up such a committee as this every once in a while so that the Dominion Elections Act can be reviewed. I understand that the chief electoral officer is constantly reviewing electoral practices, and when he feels there are changes that should be recommended he makes that fact known so that the committee can be set up and consideration given to ways to improve our election machinery.
Since the committee is to be set up and the act is to be reviewed, it seems to me that this is the occasion for members to indicate any matters which they feel should be given particular consideration. All of us in this house have had a good deal of experience with Canada's election machinery, and no doubt all of us have suggestions that we would like to make. There are a number I should like to make, but I shall confine myself on this occasion to one. 1 refer to the problem created for a great many electors in Canada by virtue of the fact that they do not happen to be in their own home constituencies on election day. In the election act there is provision for advance voting, but that privilege is accorded to a very limited number of people. It really does not fill the bill.
I think everyone will agree that, so far as the exercise of the franchise is concerned, the ideal is that it should be extended as widely as possible. Our aim should be to encourage Canadian citizens to get out and vote on election day. But the fact is that there are reasons that make it necessary for people to be away from their homes, away 80709-139J
Dominion Elections Act from their constituencies, on the day that the election happens to be held. People are sometimes away because of business. There are times, let it be said, when people are away on their holidays or vacations. When one realizes that many people in this country are tied to their work for 48, 50 or 51 weeks of the year, surely when they get one or two weeks' holidays it is a matter of importance that they get away if they possibly can. If an election falls when working people are away on their holidays, I suggest that some arrangement should be made to enable them to vote.
There are various ways in which it can be done. The simplest move to make-and I cannot understand why it was not made long ago-is to extend the right to advance voting and put it on a much broader basis. As I indicated at the start, we did not know this motion was going to be called today; therefore I do not happen to have the election act here, but I believe that advance voting is restricted to people who work for transportation companies and who are necessarily absent from their homes on election day in connection with their work. There are one or two other classes, such as fishermen and the mounted police. I hear some hon. members saying "commercial travellers", but I am not sure of that. At any rate there is obviously some doubt or uncertainty on that point. Certainly a great many people who find themselves away-frequently of necessity-on election day are not permitted to vote at the advance polls.
That is not true with respect to all elections in Canada. I know, for example, that in my own province of Manitoba the right to vote at advance polls in provincial elections is open to anyone who for any reason finds that he will have to be away on election day. No harm is done by virtue of that fact. No one abuses the privilege of democracy when he is allowed to vote in that way. I submit that the least that can be done with respect to this problem, so far as people away on election day are concerned, is that they should be allowed to vote at advance polls.
On a previous occasion when this matter was under discussion, I drew the attention of the house to the fact that there is another way in which this matter is handled in one province at any rate, and I refer to the province of British Columbia. In that province there is what is known as absentee voting. The mechanics are rather simple; if any qualified elector of the province of British Columbia is away from his home constituency on election day he may vote in whatever constituency he finds himself

Dominion Elections Act on that day. There is a special ballot for the purpose, so that he votes for one of the candidates in his own riding. The counting of absentee ballots takes place a little later than the counting of ballots cast in home constituencies and after that the final results are announced.	-
I have heard many complimentary things said about the way in which absentee voting operates in British Columbia. In order to make the picture complete, I believe I should point out that the right to vote in another constituency than one's own does not apply to persons moving about in the Vancouver or Victoria areas. For example, if your home is in one constituency in Vancouver you cannot claim the right to vote as an absentee voter in some other Vancouver constituency, but if your home is in Vancouver and you find yourself in the interior of the province on election day you do not thereby lose your vote. I submit that consideration might be given to working out something of that kind in connection with federal elections as well. I readily recognize the problem if one were to try to do it on a nation-wide basis-in other words, if an attempt were made to permit persons from Halifax to vote for the Halifax candidates of their choice anywhere in Canada; but at least it could be tried out within provincial areas.
I offer these suggestions in the hope that they will be taken into consideration by the committee. This is not the first time suggestions of this kind have been made on the floor of this house, and I believe they have been considered by similar committees on previous occasions. As yet, however, no action has been taken to alleviate the situation. I believe it is important that Canadians be encouraged to vote, and that the right to vote be accorded to them as widely as possible. The least I would hope that the committee might do this session with respect to this problem is to recommend an enlargement of the provisions with respect to advance voting.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of Ihe Opposiiion):
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND SUGGEST AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The suggestion has been made that the Secretary of State (Mr. Bradley) should explain the general intention as to the procedure to be followed, and also indicate the nature of the recommendations that have been made. Before that suggestion is disposed of, it seems to me that, after all, the main concern of every hon. member should be to make sure that the business of this house is carried on in the most expeditious and satisfactory manner. I should think it would be the desire of hon. members to give

unanimous consent to any procedure that would bring the most satisfactory results in dealing with a matter of this kind.
Surely no subject could be brought before this house for consideration which is of much greater importance to hon. members and to the people of Canada than the amendment of the act which provides for the democratic expression from time to time of the will of the people. In the motion before us there is an indication that apart from the general opinion of the members of that committee, and apart from such views as may be put forward by those asked to comprise the committee, the Secretary of State has received a number of recommendations. During the sittings of any important committee many hon. members who are not on the committee convey their opinions to members of the committee as to the subjects that should be brought forward, and give some indication of the views they feel should be expressed there. It appears that the Secretary of State has a number of recommendations of which hon. members generally are wholly unaware. I should think this would be the time for an expression of opinion as to some considerations which should receive particular attention by this committee. Without any attempt to impose the rules as a limiting factor, it would seem to me desirable that the Secretary of State should indicate the particular recommendations which will be put forward and the procedure he thinks should be followed, so that hon. members who are not on the committee will be in a position to make their recommendations to members of the committee as to what should be discussed.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND SUGGEST AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I had the honour to propose the name of the present chief electoral officer for that important post, not as a nominee of the government but as a nominee of this house, the proposal was received in this chamber with unanimous acclaim. I think we are all agreed that it is desirable that under the act the franchise shall be exercised as widely as possible, and no one would wish to insist upon any rule that unduly diminished the possibility of any elector exercising his franchise.
The chief electoral officer I am sure is objectively concerned at all times with what he feels from his experience, not only as chief electoral officer but as assistant to the chief electoral officer, may be workable. I do not think it would be in accord with the former practice, and perhaps not the right thing to do, for the government to make recommendations to the house as to what should be done under the elections act. Here
Dominion Elections Act we are endeavouring to set up a representative committee. We are bringing no pressure whatsoever upon the chief electoral officer as to the nature of his recommendations; and I would not like any of those recommended as members of this committee by the whip on this side to feel that they had any duty to the government in exercising their functions as members of that committee. It is not a matter of government and opposition; it is a matter of the general membership of the house striving to get the kind of act that will make it easier to bring to this house proper representation of the whole body of electors. I would hope that the committee would consider these recommendations which come objectively from the chief electoral officer without any thought as to how they might work to the advantage or disadvantage of one party or another.
It seems to me that those of us who will not be members of the committee will be entitled to attend and make representations directly to the committee, or have them made by someone who will be of its membership. The matter will be dealt with more expeditiously if the house defers any debate until the committee has made an investigation and submits recommendations. The recommendations of the committee will not be binding on the house, but when they are presented we shall have not only their substance but also the reasons which induced the committee to make them. We could then have a more profitable and expeditious debate than we can if we attempt now to discuss in advance recommendations which may or may not have been made to the Secretary of State by the chief electoral officer.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND SUGGEST AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to agree with the Prime Minister, because I am sure all members are anxious to produce the best election act possible. I want to make it clear that in suggesting that we should have proposals from the Secretary of State it was not my purpose to extend the debate. I thought that if we had a concise statement as to how the committee was to proceed, and some indication of the suggestions that were to be put forward, it might avoid a debate.

Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to debate this motion,, although there are certain matters connected with the elections act which I think are important. The debate, however, having been opened by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair), I see no reason why I should not add my little bit.

Dominion Elections Act
Although I agree with much of what the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said in connection with this resolution, I believe that it is in much the same position as any other resolution coming before this house for the setting up of a committee. The members of the house are free to express their opinions concerning any aspect of the act that may come before the committee.
I intend to be brief, but there are two things to which I should like to refer. One of those things will certainly have to have government approval before it can become law. In conversation with the returning officer in my own riding, Vancouver East, as well as with returning officers in other ridings in Vancouver at the last election, I found they were unanimous in insisting that they were cramped in carrying out their duties because of the smallness of the remuneration they were allowed to pay for help. I suggest that that is a matter which should come before the committee, and upon which the chief electoral officer should be in a position to guide the committee, as no doubt complaints have been made to him.
Then, there is the question of persons being unable to vote who are not in their constituencies on election day. I think I have been a member of all the election committees that have been set up by this house since I came here. This question has always been one that received a great deal of consideration by those committees. I am sure the members of the committees were anxious to extend voting privileges to those who may be absent from their ridings on election day, but the difficulty was to find a formula that would extend that advantage to those people without developing a procedure that might be abused. I believe I am correct in putting it in that way.
As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has pointed out, in the province of British Columbia we have developed a technique for allowing those who are not in their constituencies on election day to cast their ballot. I believe the formula is efficient and foolproof. It is the absentee ballot. It does not matter in what part of the province the voter happens to be on election day; if he wants to vote for the candidates in his riding he oan do so if his name is on the voters' list in the riding in which he resides. If the riding in which he lives and has his vote is a large one and, because of the distance, he is not able to be at the designated polling place in his riding, he can vote at any other polling place in the same riding. He cannot do that, of course, in the urban ridings.
I recall that in one election, I think it was in 1941, I was in the city of Prince George
[Mr. Maclnnis.l

on election day. I live in the constituency of Vancouver-Burrard, and I voted for the candidates in that constituency just as easily and just as effectively as if I had been at home on that day. I believe the method used in British Columbia can be adopted in federal elections just as easily as in provincial elections. However, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said, it might be found advisable to limit the absentee vote to the constituencies within a province.
With these few remarks, Mr. Speaker, so far as I am concerned I am quite willing to let these matters go to the committee and have them discussed there.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think there could be several improvements made in this election act. Ever since I came here in 1940 there is one amendment about which I have been concerned, and that is the one which would provide for the transferable vote. I agree with the principles set forth by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in connection with making an effective act for the individual elector. From experience, however, I think there is plenty of proof that we should have the transferable vote.
In the general election of 1949, for instance, there were 121 members elected by a minority of the votes cast in their respective ridings; that is a very large percentage of the total number of members in this house. As a matter of fact, during that same election supporters of the present government, which has such an overwhelming majority, were elected to approximately seventy-five per cent of the seats in this house with less than fifty per cent of the vote which was polled across the country. I believe those figures were issued by the chief electoral officer at the time. I am not complaining about that and saying that the election act should be revised now, because that has happened on other occasions. But in a modern democratic nation we should reduce this sort of gamble as much as we can. It is important that this committee should recommend to the house an amendment to provide for the transfer of votes, so that if there is a multiplicity of candidates in a riding a candidate must receive a majority of the votes cast before he can be elected. I believe that change should be made in the interests of modern democracy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not rise to raise a point of order at this time as I did before. I rise now to take part in the debate, in order to suggest to the Secretary of State (Mr. Bradley) that, in view of the present voting hours provided for under our election act, a large and, if I may say so, growing group of voters are

virtually disfranchised. I refer more particularly to those who are now in that greatly increased class of people who commute from their residences to their places of work.
I suppose it will not be any news to hon. members to be told that there are now in Canada many people who are commuting from places as far as fifty miles or more away from their work. To travel these distances takes a considerable length of time, even if they use a motorcar, thus making for flexibility of hours which may meet their convenience in special instances. But there are large numbers of people-and a great number in my own riding-who use the train service morning and night in going to and coming from their work. What it means is this, if they are to continue to use that train service: they cannot stay long enough in the morning to vote, and they cannot get back early enough at night to do so. The committee ought to make a thorough study of that question; because, following up what the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) so aptly said a few minutes ago, I fancy it is the desire of every member of this house that there should be, under an act of this kind, as little inconvenience, lack of accommodation and disfranchisement as possible.
I should also point out, Mr. Speaker, that this group of people to whom I have referred is rapidly increasing in numbers in many sections of Canada. What may not have been a problem ten, fifteen or twenty years ago has now become an acute one which these commuters and suburbanites feel is a matter of discrimination with regard to their franchise. I hope the committee will deal with that matter.
Before I sit down, inasmuch as the minister did not make a statement at the opening of this debate may I suggest that he take the opportunity of doing so before the debate closes, and of at least disclosing the information, with regard to amendments that was given to him by the chief electoral officer. When he does so, we will follow the principle laid down by the Prime Minister and will not regard him as a cabinet minister but just as one of the rest of us.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to report that agreement has been reached with the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan for

Inquiries of the Ministry establishing a large R.C.A.F. bombing and gunnery range roughly 100 miles northeast of Edmonton. The range will cover an area of several thousand square miles, and is necessitated by the high speed of modern jet aircraft and the long range of their weapons, including rockets and cannon, which result in a large increase in the danger area. speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SECURITY AGREEMENT
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Yesterday President Truman announced plans for working out a security agreement between the United States and Australia and New Zealand which apparently is to lead to a full-scale Pacific pact comparable to the North Atlantic alliance. Will the minister tell the house where Canada fits into this picture?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SECURITY AGREEMENT
speechtext:
The statement which was made by President Truman yesterday in Washington-and I believe statements were also made in New Zealand and Australia- referred to a proposed arrangement between the governments of Australia, New Zealand and the United States for mutual security pursuant to articles 51 and 52 of the United Nations charter. The Canadian government has been kept closely informed of those negotiations, and we have already indicated to the governments of Australia and New Zealand that we welcome them as an important contribution to the defence of freedom by increasing stability in the area to be covered by these arrangements. That area was referred to by the Australian minister of external affairs in a statement to the house of representatives in Canberra on March 14 last, when he said-and I am quoting from Mr. Spender's statement:
The objective has been to obtain an arrangement which will benefit the whole of the western Pacific area, guaranteeing friendly aid and protection in the event of a renewed threat of attack.
Yesterday in his statement President Truman did say that these arrangements constitute initial steps, not, as I understood him, necessarily to a Pacific pact, but initial steps in the consolidation of peace in that area. If these negotiations are extended to cover anything like a Pacific pact analogous to the North Atlantic pact, naturally the Canadian government would be interested; but we have received no indication that these additional negotiations are going to take place.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext:
Last Monday the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) asked if there had been a recent order in council relating to outside employment for civil servants. I indicated that there was such an order, and promised to give a statement at a later date, which I now wish to do.
Order in council P.C. 3/1440 lays down certain principles relating to outside employment undertaken by civil servants. Earlier orders in council dating back to 1925 had laid down the general principle that no fulltime civil servant earning more than $1,600 a year could engage in any outside gainful employment without the express approval of treasury board. Literally applied, this meant that no civil servant could, for example, receive payment for serving as an organist in a church, or even acting as a baby sitter, without prior approval by treasury board. This was manifestly inoperable and, in fact, the regulation has not been generally enforced.
After full discussion the national joint council of the public service of Canada recommended the new regulations which have been incorporated in P.C. 3/1440.
In effect, the new regulations define certain classes of prohibited employment; for example, where the employee would make use of confidential information acquired in the course of his duties.
In all other respects the control of outside employment has now been passed to the deputy heads of the departments, who may lay down principles applicable to their respective departments. Subject to such departmental rules as the deputy head may lay down, a civil servant may engage in non-prohibited outside employment so long as it does not impair his efficiency in the public service. Where a deputy head is of the opinion that outside employment is impairing the efficiency of the employee's regular duties, he may direct the employee to cease or to limit such outside employment.
I shall table a copy of the order in council, if it has not already been tabled.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, April 18, consideration of the motion of Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood), and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today at 12.30 the ears of the whole world were tuned to Washington to hear an address by that great soldier, General Douglas MacArthur. His classic speech will long be remembered, not only by our American cousins but throughout the entire world where freedom still survives today. His remark that the American concept of human liberties was the best yet devised and his remark that the hopes and aspirations of the human race centred in the historic chamber from which he was speaking may to the same degree apply to Canada and to this chamber.
The warning of General MacArthur that you cannot appease communism in Asia may well be repeated in this house. His reference to the dignity of all mankind should be remembered. His warning of there being no substitute for victory or a sham peace laying the base for future demands should be well heeded by all pacifists and isolationists in Canada. His reference to prolonged indecision, political indecision and the lack of reinforcements for the American army when he called for reinforcements may well be pondered over by this government.
Those of us who were here in the 1944 parliament well remember the tragic price that Canada had to pay for the lack of trained reinforcements for service overseas. There are many in Canada today who feel that the strength of our armed forces is much too low in view of the world situation. I sincerely hope that the reason for this is not the result of political indecision.
In taking part in the budget debate I wish to refer only briefly to certain matters which have been discussed already by other members. It has been pointed out already to the

The Budget-Mr. G. S. White Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that corporation profits during the past year have been at an all-time high, while the net income of the primary producers has been decreasing. While the minister has imposed an additional 20 per cent surtax on corporations, I think he will find that at the end of the year when their statements are issued profits for 1951 will be even higher than in 1950. In the past it has been proven that when additional taxes are imposed on corporations it simply means that the price of the product or manufactured article is raised and the increase is passed on to the consumer. After all, there is nothing to prevent a manufacturer of washing machines, radios, or anything else from setting his own prices. As the Minister of Finance pointed out a moment ago, he has nothing whatever to do with setting the retail price of gasoline. Neither has the minister nor the government anything to do with setting the price of any product. Therefore I submit that, so far as many corporations are concerned, these additional taxes will simply be passed on to the consumer.
Many speakers have already referred to the 20 per cent increase in personal income tax. In his remarks the minister indicated that he was pleased and took credit for not lowering the exemption. If the minister wanted to take credit for doing something, he could have easily increased the exemptions to $1,500 and $3,000 respectively, and he would have received cheers and credit all across the country. The minister should remember that when the exemptions were set at their present figures the value of the Canadian dollar was much higher than it is today, and the cost of living index was much lower than it is at the present time.
The so-called luxury tax is most unfair in many aspects. I for one often wonder who the experts are who decide what items are to be classed as luxuries. We live in a cold climate, so let us take furs, for example. Under the system of taxation it does not matter whether the fur in question costs $75, $200 or $500. They are all subject to the same rate of tax. The same applies to a watch. It does not make any difference whether it costs $50, $300 or $500. The same scale of taxation applies to many other items which today are classed as luxuries. I suggest to the minister that in the taxation of these so-called luxury items some limit or line be established whereby the tax would only apply to such articles when they exceeded a certain price. There are many other items classed as luxuries today such as clocks, luggage, pens, and so on. It is rather difficult to understand how the minister can justify

taxing these items of ordinary everyday use and necessity when at the same time expensive articles of furniture, oriental rugs and oil paintings are not taxed.
The new tax of 15 per cent on washing machines and other electrical equipment is in my opinion most unfortunate. In Ontario at least the hydro commission each year builds hundreds and hundreds of miles of new hydro lines. For the first time many new consumers are able to obtain the benefits of cheap power and the great benefits that flow from the use of the many electrical appliances we have today. Naturally these people, who for the first time are hooked up with hydro, have no electrical equipment of any kind, and today they find that on top of the present very high price for electrical equipment they are faced with an additional 15 per cent tax. It seems to me that many articles for which electricity is used are too high today. Take, for example, the ordinary electric stove, which is not a complicated piece of machinery. Nevertheless the average price in Ontario, without the additional 2 per cent sales tax and the 15 per cent excise tax, is $300. The same high prices apply to practically every other type of electrical equipment. Young married couples furnishing their first home will find that these taxes on absolute necessities impose great hardship. These young people are faced with the necessity of buying electrical equipment not because of the fact that the minister has put a tax on stoves but because in the great majority of cases electricity is the only thing used for cooking and other purposes.
I agree with the remarks made the other evening by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) with respect to medical deductions for income tax purposes. I think the minister could well afford to adopt the suggestion made by the hon. member and allow all medical expenses as a deduction. In my opinion the present method of allowing the amount over 4 per cent of the net income, with the provision that such figure is not to exceed $750 for a single person and $1,000 for a married person, should be abolished. I would point out to the minister that when the 4 per cent provision was inserted in the income tax law hospital charges, nursing fees, doctors' fees, surgeons' fees and all other fees pertaining to sickness were much lower than they are at the present time. I know from personal experience that I have had occasion many times to examine medical bills both in connection with estates and for income tax purposes, and I am always amazed at how much it costs to be ill or to have an operation. I think the change suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg

North Centre is very fair, and is worthy of serious consideration by the minister.
I should also like to bring to the attention of the minister an item appearing in the brief submitted by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce on the 23rd of February, 1951, having to do with the Dominion Succession Duty Act. The submission in the brief is as follows:
The chamber reiterates its protest that in estates over $50,000 the federal government levies succession duties not only on the excess of $50,000 but on the initial $50,000, thus establishing an inequality of exemption, and setting up in the Succession Duty Act a discriminatory provision.
It is pointed out in the submission that there is inequality of exemption, and I suggest to the minister that his department could well afford to amend the act so that there would be an allowance of $50,000 in all estates thereby removing this inequality of exemption. I am sure the loss suffered by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) would be very small.
As the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) is here, I wonder if he has seen the very interesting picture that appeared on the front page of the Ottawa Journal of yesterday. It shows the foundation for the new printing bureau across the river in Hull, and the heading is, "How's the Fishing?" Then there is this comment:
Boaters and hopeful anglers this morning were "cruising down the river" on a newly formed body of water in the excavation of the government printing bureau in Hull. The water was 19 feet deep, and was formed by the backing up of flood-swollen Brewery creek.
I presume it is water; it does not say it was beer.
Works department pumping crews this afternoon were pumping the water back into the creek so that the work on the superstructure could go on. The 13-acre printing bureau site cost the federal government more than $800,000 in expropriation payments.
I should like to suggest to the minister that if he is having difficulty with the location over there he might move the location to my riding. There is plenty of good high land and the foundations could be built on solid rock. The cost of the land would not be anything like $800,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext:
I will take it into
consideration.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I
must say that if you come up there you will not be able to fish out the windows, but I can assure you that you will not have far to go to enjoy the best fishing to be found anywhere in Canada.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak briefly on the dairy industry in Canada. I want to
The Budget-Mr. G. S. White commend the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) on the very fine, fair presentation he made in this house on behalf of the industry last Monday. I agree with, and concur in every way in, the remarks made by the hon. member, which will be found at page 2071 of Hansard. For a long period the county in which I live has been a great producer of cheese. For many years it produced more cheese than any other county in Ontario. The famous Black Diamond cheese, manufactured and cured in this county, is becoming famous in many countries, and every year the demand in the United States is increasing. The importance of the cheese industry to this county is indicated by the fact that the first producer storage plant to provide cheese curing, storage and laboratory facilities was erected at Belleville.
Since Hastings is an agricultural county it is only natural that the farm producers should be greatly concerned about any fall in prices which affects their products. The very serious inequity as between urban and rural producers which existed at the outset of the war could not be cured1 by wartime controls. In order to get production at that time labour were given practically everything they asked, but at the same time farm products were strictly controlled. It is quite clear now that the unavoidable wartime controls and the unnecessary peacetime compulsory marketing and political prices since the war have cost the Canadian farm producers hundreds of millions of dollars, and it seems to me the government should take some action to reimburse the farm producers of eastern Ontario and Quebec for the losses they have sustained.
Apparently the government recognized that it had some obligation in the matter. I will not say it was a legal obligation; it could only be a moral obligation, but already they have approved the payment of $65 million to reimburse western farmers who sold their product under practically the same conditions.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That was just a token payment.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It
shows the advantage to any group of producers in Canada in being well organized and exerting great pressure on the government, as well as having their members in the house make insistent demands in their behalf. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) went to England to see what could be done to obtain further moneys for Canada to pay for our wheat. He was unable to make any settlement, however, and as a result of his visit the general public of Canada have had to pay $65 million as a bonus to western farm producers. The farmers of eastern Ontario

The Budget-Mr. G. S. White and Quebec certainly will have to pay their share of this $65 million, despile the fact that during the same period their products were being shipped to Britain at much lower prices than prevailed in the United States. The cheese and bacon of eastern Ontario and Quebec were requisitioned and confiscated, and the producer had absolutely nothing to say in the matter. If there is an obligation, even only morally, to pay the western wheat producers, there is exactly the same moral obligation to make up to the producers of eastern Ontario and Quebec the losses they sustained on the sale of their products. And if the payment of $65 million was made on a moral basis only, then I suggest that the whole issue of the post-war food contracts with Britain should be reopened and reviewed.
During the war there was never any question of a surplus of farm products. The government encouraged farmers to increase production of every kind. The farmers did increase their stock and their acreage, and this at a time when farm labour was scarce and machinery was hard to get and very expensive. The production of foodstuffs was greatly increased, both for civilian use and for the members of the armed services. But during the war years farm products were strictly controlled, and the farmer had1 no price tag on them. During the same period, however, industry did have a price tag on its products. In many cases industry operated on a cost plus basis, and that is the way industry operates today. There is a price tag on every article turned out, and' that price tag makes sure that the manufacturer gets back his cost of production plus a very fair profit.
In his remarks the hon. member for Lanark gave the results of a survey in his county, which showed that in one year the average farmer lost $147 on his milk production. In its report in 1947 the Ontario royal commission on milk showed that it cost $2.69 to produce one hundred pounds of milk for cheese, while the milk producer received in return only from $1.95 to $2.10. I should like to quote a few paragraphs from this report. Under the heading "Price and cost of production" it says:
The farmer producing fluid milk for consumption in towns and cities of the province is as much entitled to a fair return for his work as a consumer who works in a factory or an office. If up to the present time, through lack of sufficiently effective organization, he has not been able to make his demands felt, that is not a reason for asking him to produce milk for the fluid market at prices less than his cost plus a reasonable profit. He is primarily entitled to the costs of producing milk and to a fair profit for that labour.

In regard to milk and cheese the commission found these very interesting facts:
The results of an over-all survey made by the accountants attached to the commission . . . show an average net cost of producing one hundred pounds of cheese milk in 1946 to be $2.34, to which an administrative allowance of 35 cents was added, making a total cost, including administrative allowance, of $2.69 for one hundred pounds of cheese milk.
At the time of the inquiry . . . the return to the cheese milk producer was estimated at between $1.95 and $2.10 ... If the average figure is one of general application, as I believe it is, it would seem to substantiate the contention brought forward by the cheese producers association that the price structure existing at that time did not permit a return to the farmer sufficient to pay his cost of production and give him even a modest profit.
If it cost $2.69 to produce one hundred pounds of cheese milk in 1946, certainly it will cost a great deal more in 1951, because as everyone knows the cost of labour and materials has greatly increased. Yet, so far as 1950 is concerned, the milk producer was only receiving approximately $2 per hundred for his milk. In 1950 the cheese producer received 28 cents at seaboard for his product under a contract made by the Minister of Agriculture. The cheese producer had no say in the matter. Additional freight rates and increased cost of production will no doubt further reduce the returns to the cheese producer in 1951.
I would point out that since 1941 over 150 cheese factories in the province of Ontario have closed. In the district in which I live I know of three factories which will not operate during the 1951 season. Speaking to the farmers who have formerly sent milk to these factories, they tell me they will not continue sending milk for prices similar to those which they received in 1950. In many cases the production of milk is simply a sideline. Many farmers will -not continue to produce milk for the production of cheese -at a loss. I would point out that cheese, butter and other farm products were most important during the war for food for both armed forces and civilians. Surely as a defence measure for the future at least the remaining cheese factories should be kept in operation.
I recall that only a short time ago a protest was made in this house against certain cheap foreign shirts from Japan that were being dumped on the Canadian market. Apparently the Canadian textile industry had enough influence or brought enough pressure to bear on the proper authorities to have the importation stopped. If it is necessary, Mr. Speaker, for the textile industry to have protection of that type, surely then it is not unreasonable to ask that the dairy producers have some sort of protection from

substitutes shipped into this country, and then manufactured into food products which take the place of natural food products.
On Monday last the Minister of Agriculture stated that no decision had yet been reached as to the price of butter for this year. No doubt the minister and his department have received many letters, telegrams and petitions

as many members have-from farm groups and cream associations requesting that a floor price for butter be set at 62 cents a pound. I for one hope the minister will see fit to recommend a floor price for butter of 62 cents a pound.
So far as cheese is concerned, I fail to see how our producers can operate on even smaller margins of profit if the price in 1951 is less than 32 cents a pound, and that f.o.b. the factory. I should like to ask the Minister of Agriculture a question. Does he feel that the price of 28 cents a pound at seaboard received by the cheese producers of Ontario in 1950 was a fair and reasonable price, and a price at which the milk producer for cheese could operate at a profit?
As I have mentioned to the minister before, there are many veterans in my county who used their gratuities and re-establishment credit to set themselves up in farming. These veterans have heavy commitments to meet in the future, and if they are to be successfully re-established in our peacetime economy they must receive better returns for their farm products. Not long ago a dairy farmer was one whose main objective was to produce and sell milk, and his farm was run to that end. Today the average dairy farmer, apart from the one who produces whole milk for large communities, simply means a farmer who keeps cows as a sideline. It could not be otherwise, considering the prices of manufactured milk during the past few years and the rising cost of everything that a farmer must purchase, including labour. Any man dependent wholly upon his milk cheque during the past few years would have to be pretty good to keep his head above water.
The dairymen in eastern Ontario and Quebec have been kept in business by a thriving export business for dairy cattle, and the high prices paid for any kind of animal that could be used as meat. I know that in my county every week in the year there are buyers from New York state who are anxious to buy dairy cattle. I admit that the prices are good, in fact the prices are extra good. Unfortunately every year the number of cattle in the county is seriously decreasing. No doubt there are some farmers who never sell on the export market, but they have a ready sale to other farmers and
The Budget-Mr. G. S. White to local butchers willing to buy all their young cattle for beef. So far as the dairy farmer is concerned, this is not good. It has made him content to accept low prices for manufactured milk, such as those prevailing last summer. It has also made him indifferent to the fight against substitutes for milk and cream. This has been most noticeable lately. The use of substitutes for milk and cream strikes at the very core of the dairy industry, not just butter but every other product that is made from milk.
Some time ago it was reported that in the city of Toronto alone the large bakeries had discontinued their daily purchases of hundreds of cans of thick cream. They are now using a filled product, the chief ingredient of which is imported into Canada. The uses to which this imported filling can be put are practically endless. Certainly, it could be used in cheese and probably will be in the future if something is not done to assist this industry. For the past ten years there has been no problem connected with the sale of pork and cheese. Both these products were taken by the British, but not always under satisfactory conditions. It now appears as though this whole method of trading and doing business with the British would end unless there is another war. It can practically be taken for granted now that a cheese contract for 1951 based on 1950 prices will be little more than a farce.
So far as cheese and bacon are concerned the British want all we can give them, but they feel that they cannot afford to pay the prices which are necessary to secure those supplies today. A curious sidelight on this aspect is that, while the British are not willing to pay the going prices for our food or raw materials, their own charges for manufactured articles exported to Canada are very high. If you look about in the stores you will find that everything of British manufacture is expensive. No one will ever find a bargain. Occasionally that is a little hard to understand.
A short time ago an article appeared in the Farm Journal under this heading: "More Talk of Wanting Cheese and Bacon". The article reads in part as follows:
There has been another article in the daily papers to the effect that the United Kingdom "wants" more cheese and bacon from Canada in 1951 than she obtained this year, and again the suggestion- she was unwilling to increase the price.
It is about time this sort of talk ceased and things got down to a businesslike basis.
Things are in a bad- enough mess in the Canadian-dairy industry without this sort of talk. The best course would be for Mr. Gardiner to stop it all by telling the British that if they want cheese and bacon they should go into the open market, and pay for it as Canadians have to pay. If he wants to be generous and big hearted he can make any kind of

The Budget-Mr. G. S. White a "contract" he wishes, and be prepared to pay a subsidy. He should not again expect Canadian producers to foot the bill.
The article continues:
Add to the competition from foreign oils the fact that cheese and now powdered milk products are coming into this country from Australia and New Zealand, whose production costs are evidently a lot lower than here in Canada. It is being rumoured that New Zealand whole milk powder will undersell the Canadian product by six cents a pound.
Then there is the riddle of butter. Despite the inroads of margarine on the butter industry all signs point now to a shortage of domestic stocks of butter next spring. The production situation on the prairies is particularly bad, and much of the surplus comes from there.
We are likely to see imports of butter into Canada by next spring. Which means that every Canadian dairy product, except whole milk, will have competition from outside sources on a price basis. It is doubtful if such a situation ever faced the whole industry here before.
And certain new developments in the canned milk trade do not leave even the whole milk people free from the threat of a new kind of competition.
I would ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) if in 1951 we are to have a repetition of our own cheese being requisitioned at 28 cents at seaboard and the permitting of New Zealand cheese at 32 cents to 34 cents to be imported into the country in order to meet our domestic needs. The recent ruling of the Supreme Court of Canada allowing the sale of margarine was another blow to the dairy industry. Certain Canadian companies are making huge fortunes out of the manufacture of margarine. It will be recalled that in this house it was often said that if the manufacture of margarine was permitted in Canada the Canadian farmer would benefit because he would be able to produce certain crops from which oil could be produced; but we all know that there is no Canadian product that we could produce that could compete with the imported edible oils produced in many cases under conditions which we in Canada could only class as slave labour.
It was pointed out by my colleague the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) that over two million Canadians depend on the dairy industry for their livelihood. He asked a pertinent question, namely, how many Canadians were employed in the manufacture of margarine. This large number of Canadians who depend on the dairy industry for their livelihood supply a large part of the purchasing power for Canadian goods. One wonders if all this is to be swept aside; if the dairy industry, which has always been one of the basic industries of this country, is gradually to fade out; and if our butter, cheese and other dairy products are, in the future, to be made out of substitutes imported from abroad.

The minister has not yet announced any contract for cheese for 1951 or whether or not cheese will be requisitioned. At the present time it certainly appears that the production of cheese in 1951 in Ontario will reach another all-time low. Everyone knows that producing herds in Canada are at a low figure; and in the event of war it will take a long time to build up those herds. Surely it is just as much part of the program for defence to build up our food producing defences as it is to buildj up our military defences; for certainly, if war comes again, Canada will be expected to provide huge supplies of food products for our allies, for the armed forces and for the civilians.
I trust, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Agriculture, even at this late date, will see fit to recommend to his cabinet colleagues, as he did before, that something should be paid as compensation to the cheese and bacon producers of eastern Canada, and especially to those in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, in order to compensate them in some way for the loss they suffered on the sale of their dairy products to the United Kingdom during the same period that the wheat was sold. As I pointed out before, if there was any moral obligation to pay the wheat producers, there is the same obligation to pay a like amount to the bacon and cheese producers. However, if the minister will not recommend any such payment I would ask him at some time to explain to the house how he could justify the $65 million paid when no legal obligation existed. If no payment is to be made-and frankly, I for one do not expect that any such payment will be made-the citizens of Canada can only regard the payment of $65 million to the western farmers as a well-organized raid on the federal treasury, which raid was led and engineered by the Minister of Agriculture.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in joining in this budget debate, I wish to add my appreciation to that already expressed by previous speakers of the able and patriotic attention which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) continues to give to his exacting duties. His presentation of this budget again demonstrates that he has a wide knowledge of the economic situation in Canada and is giving us wise leadership in the financial field. I consider this budget to be a realistic one, considering the present international situation. It is not a pleasant budget, but I believe it is not an unfair one.
No one can quarrel with the minister's statement that, in the framing of this budget, he was guided by concern over two vital

matters, namely, the pursuit of peace and the control of inflation. These matters are the first concern of all of us. We are ready to make severe sacrifices in order to attain them both. His review of Canada's economic activities was constructive. He told us of our huge national production. Last year it amounted to about $18 billion. We find that there are 130,000 more people employed than there were a year ago, in spite of the unemployment situation which was so sorrowfully predicted by the members of the opposition. Our international trade is in good condition. We maintained the volume of our export trade. Our imports increased to some extent. This is a condition which we all welcome, because we are now importing more from the British empire, thereby earning for the British dollars which they greatly need. I believe that this change in the direction of our trade is a good thing for the entire British empire. I am pleased to see that we have a balanced budget, with a surplus of $203 million. Members of the opposition have objected to having a surplus; but in my humble opinion, running a government is much like running an individual business. If you are in debt, it is wise to pay off that debt. I do not consider that it is inflationary. I insist that it is antiinflationary, as the Minister of Finance has stated it to be. The hon. member for Eglin-ton (Mr. Fleming), as reported at page 2107 of Hansard, had this to say with regard to a balanced budget:
The minister has said he wants to balance his budget. I do not think a single member of this house will have any disagreement with that professed objective. We all wish to see this budget balanced this year; . . .
Later on he continues, on the same page:
I submit, sir, that the first duty of a minister of finance in submitting a budget is to give the house a true estimate, and as accurate an estimate as can possibly be devised, of the expected revenues accruing from the various fields of taxation.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that our present Minister of Finance did just that. How could anyone, one year ago, predict the great buoyancy of revenue which we experienced during 1950? Certainly the members of the opposition did not make any such prediction. Had the minister followed the advice of the members of the opposition, when they were predicting early in 1950 prolonged unemployment and a serious recession of business, he would have been forced to conclude that even higher taxes than he recommended at that time would be necessary to ensure a balanced budget.
I believe that the reduction of our national debt to the extent of nearly $2 billion over
The Budget-Mr. Robertson the last five years is a remarkable achievement. When we remember that the interest charges of that amount would be in the neighbourhood of $70 million, I think we have made a great contribution in giving tax relief to the people of our country.
I also believe that the government has a notable achievement in the field of economy. We have reduced our estimates on nondefence expenditures by $35 million, and this in spite of the fact that we have had increased salaries, increased wages, and the fact that we are giving to old age pensions, family allowances and the provincial governments $40 million more than last year, over which we have no control.
The members of the opposition cry extravagance. I should like to read some of their statements. The hon. member for Eglinton said at page 2109 of Hansard of April 17:
Is there any extravagance? Well, sir, time alone prevents my giving in greater detail some of these examples of extravagance; but let me remind you of just one or two examples. Last year, my colleague, the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), put before the house the startling-yes, shocking-fact that expenditures on travelling, publicity and sundries in the estimates of that year totalled $49 million, exhibiting a startling increase year by year, as the government spending machine has demanded more and more oil. What do we find this year has been accomplished by the government in this so-called "economy drive" in relation to travelling expenses? Well, we find, sir, that the Minister of Finance reports an increase in the appropriation for travelling and removal expenses, going up from $27,786,602 in the year 1950-51 to a figure of $36,300,109 for this current fiscal year. Let me remind you, sir, that the figures last year included defence expenditures as well.
Now, Mr. Speaker, when I looked into this matter further I found that there had been an increase over last year of approximately $8,522,507; but when I checked it further I found that of this increase $8,378,108 could be charged to national defence and defence construction. That means that the shocking disclosure which the hon. member for Eglinton gave to this house shows that the government did increase the expenses of travelling to the extent of approximately $140,000; and when we look into these expenditures further we find that nearly the whole of this sum has been necessary in increased expenditure of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and we all know how necessary in times of threatened war an increase in the activity of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is. There we have the startling and shocking disclosure that the hon. member for Eglinton has used to impress this house that this government did greatly increase its expenditures on travelling.
When we come to the matter of printing I know that there is an increase this year of some $775,279. Yet the increase in printing

The Budget-Mr. Robertson on behalf of national defence and the Department of Defence Production is indeed greater than that amount. That shows, Mr. Speaker, how much we can depend upon the charges made by some members of the opposition.
I have this further quotation from Hansard. Speaking on April 17, at page 2097 of Hansard, the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) said:
I wish I had time to enumerate the many instances of wasteful expenditure of money that should rightfully have been saved for the taxpayers.
This comes from the hon. member who asked many more millions of dollars for the wheat farmers of Canada. I would suggest that he should talk to his deskmate because they certainly do not agree on the wheat policy.
Then we heard much of government extravagance on publicity and publications, and hon. members of the opposition singled out the Department of National Health and Welfare for this attack. I happen to be a medical man and I stand here and say that the money spent on such publications has been spent in the best interests of Canada. We know that greater and greater emphasis is being placed on preventive medicine. We believe that we can save much money and much human suffering if we can prevent disease rather than to try to cure it; and there is no better way to bring to the people of Canada the need for preventive medicine and what they can do to enjoy good health than these publications which come from the Department of National Health and Welfare.
We know that we are making progress against that dreaded disease cancer, but we know that one of our great difficulties in dealing with this matter is the ignorance and fear which exist in the minds of the people of Canada. These publications can bring a true picture to the people of Canada, and they can derive much benefit from them, and they know where they can come to seek relief from that dreaded disease. The same can be said of many other diseases. I say that the money which is being spent on these publications is being well spent.
Last year we had a very entertaining afternoon when the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) produced some pamphlets which he had picked up from the Post Office Department, and he made some dreadful charges that the Post Office Department was spending thousands of dollars on such publications. When we learned the whole truth from the Postmaster General (Mr. Rinfret) the next day we learned that the huge sum of $2,000 had been spent on these publications, and we learned also what a good purpose those 	. ft 1 I

publications were serving. There again, Mr. Speaker, we have an exposure of the lack of details in the charges which members of the opposition use to attack the government on the extravagance subject. I maintain that the best proof of the efficiency of this government in financial affairs is to be found in the fact that little or no factual criticism has been produced by opposition members. They may tell us that they have not time to go into these things, but I am sure that the rules of the house give every hon. member all the opportunity he needs to bring forth factual criticism of the expenditures of this government.
