subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-this session answered the challenge of the leader of the opposition of this reckless expenditure of money by going over the estimates item by item and asking any hon. member of the opposition to tell him what he wished to see deleted, and I did not see any one of those hon. members getting up in his place and saying: Let us cut this out.
Coming back to the budget itself, I must say that labour is very pleased to note that union dues are to be allowed as a deduction from income tax. I attended a meeting of labour some months ago and they told me that they felt that this was an unfair tax that they were paying. I agreed with them at that time and assured them I would do what I could to have this corrected. I regret that I was not in the house because of illness when the resolution was presented asking that union dues be not subject to taxation. If I had been here I certainly would have voted in favour of such a resolution.
I regret the need of having to place in the budget a 15 per cent tax on certain household goods, particularly stoves. I realize that in imposing this tax on stoves the minister was not thinking of the revenue that would be derived therefrom but was using this as an anti-inflationary move. It is anti-inflationary because the government is trying to conserve steel for more essential purposes, but I would hope that as soon as this inflationary pressure declines the government will do away with the taxes on stoves, refrigerators and other necessary household articles.

The international situation is still of great concern to all of us. Only the good judgment and cool courage of the leaders of the free world has stopped the Korean war from becoming a full-scale war. We are indeed proud of the part which our own leaders, particularly the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), have played in this cause of peace. I am sure they have our hearty support.
We are much interested in the critical situation which has developed in the United States where it has become necessary for the President to recall that famed soldier. General MacArthur, from command in the Far East. I wish to associate myself with what the hon. member who preceded me said about General MacArthur. I believe that he is one of the outstanding leaders of the free world. I deprecate what was said in this house about Gerferal MacArthur by an hon. member not long ago. I think it reflected little credit on that hon. member or on this house.
We had the privilege of hearing General MacArthur today and I am sure that he has proved beyond any doubt that he is one of the outstanding men of this generation. I personally support the President in what he has done because I believe that as one of the bases of democratic government there should be full control over the military.
We who are completely uninformed on what is going on in the inner circles must be prepared to give our full support to the great men who are leading us today. But I think we also have the right to demand that there shall be no appeasement in this present situation.
Not long ago President Truman in a broadcast revealed that before the Korean war Moscow-trained officers instructed spies and soldiers that the plan was to liberate all Asia, crush the United States and accomplish the long awaited world revolution. The whole communist imperialism, said the President, is back of the attack on peace in the Far East. It was the Soviet union that trained and equipped the North Koreans for aggression. The Chinese communists massed forty-four well-trained and well-equipped divisions on the Korean frontier. These were the troops they threw into battle when the North Korean communists were beaten.
In view of that statement I trust it is not an idle hope to expect to be able to separate Peking from Moscow. I certainly agree with the Secretary of State for External Affairs when he said in a broadcast not long ago, I believe from Lake Success, that the free nations of the world must do everything in
The Budget-Mr. Robertson their power to prevent another great war. He said that if we are to have another war it was most important that we have overwhelming public support for our cause. I think that that is vital for our security and our survival.
I hope sincerely that history is not repeating itself and that in asking us to take stronger action against the enemy General MacArthur is not another Churchill crying in vain in an effort to awaken the democratic nations to their real danger. I ask our leaders to weigh that possibility and I hope that any decision they make will be governed by that. We have a right to ask of our leaders that there be no mistake in this matter because it is far too vital to permit a second chance.
I was much interested in the discussion which took place in this house last Friday with regard to the St. Lawrence waterway development. One could not help but be struck by the fact that hon. members from the maritimes of all political parties objected to the construction of the St. Lawrence waterway. One can well appreciate the worry that those members might have at feeling that the construction of such a seaway would interfere with the economic well-being of their part of the country. I cannot help but feel that their fears are unfounded. I believe that if this development goes through the whole economy of Canada will profit, and it will also be of benefit to the people of the maritimes.
I know the vast majority of the people in my -riding look forward to the development of the St. Lawrence waterway. They think it will be advantageous to their part of the country to have ocean-going boats in the great lakes. They know the value they will receive from the development of electric power and they appreciate the urgency of the development of this project from a defence point of view. Therefore I feel that I can tell the house that the people in central Ontario welcome this project.
I note the railway brotherhoods have submitted a brief to the government against the development of the St. Lawrence seaway. I can understand that they are worried that the development of this project may interfere with their livelihood. But I know also that the heads of both the railroads in Canada are behind the development of the St. Lawrence waterway. I am sure that they are interested in the welfare of their own employees as well as of the railroads. If I did not believe that, I could not support the construction of this project because many of my best friends in Cobourg are members

The Budget-Mr. Robertson of the railway brotherhoods and I could not recommend anything to this house that might prejudice their livelihood.
I believe that this project will mean much to the development of the ports on the great lakes. We in Cobourg look forward to the day when ocean-going ships will come direct to our town. We have one of the finest harbours on the great lakes. Contrary to what was said the other night by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Fulford), that there was no way of keeping these ports open in the wintertime, I can tell the house that we have no difficulty in maintaining our harbour in operation throughout the year. We in this house and in all parts of Canada are concerned about the procrastination that takes place in the United States whenever the St. Lawrence waterway development is mentioned. Whenever the matter is brought before congress powerful interests seem able to scuttle the project. In a United States paper I noticed the following:
In Washington last week a daily program of government activities published by the United States chamber of commerce carried this eyebrow-lifting item:	"Monday. April 2, hearings of the St. Lawrence seaway to continue at least ten years." It should have said "days" but at week's end many capitol hill newsmen thought the typographical error might have been more factual than funny.
I am pleased that the Canadian government has already expressed its support of this project, and I hope that in the near future we will find that the better people in the United States are able to secure ratification of it by the United States congress. I know that this development will mean much to the people of both Canada and the United States.
Very briefly I should like to urge the government to take what action lies in their power to decentralize industry. We in Canada are fortunate in having a country of such wide extent. It makes it more difficult for an enemy to wipe out our defences, and it also makes it easier for us to defend our country. I have been worried by the fact that industry seems to crowd into some of the larger centres in Canada, particularly Toronto, Windsor and Montreal. I believe that this is unwise because we do not know what fifty years from now may bring. We cannot imagine how destructive and powerful the weapons of those days may turn out to be. Therefore I think it is very bad for industry to crowd into narrow sectors. I think this is one of the ways that we might respond to the appeal of members from the maritimes. If the government can encourage industry to move to the maritimes I think that would be a good thing to do. I am pleased at the fact that the government is already placing defence projects over wide areas in Canada.


I also believe that there are many small communities in Ontario which offer wonderful sites for the construction of such projects. I am thinking particularly of course of my own county of Northumberland where we have many wonderful sites, a high standard of labour and excellent transportation facilities, in fact all that any industry would wish in order to establish a plant. Not only would it have the advantage of benefiting industry itself, but it would also mean much to the people in the smaller communities. It would make unnecessary the removal of many of our young people from the smaller centres to the large cities as is the case under the present situation.
There is one other very important matter to which I should like to direct your attention. We hear much these days of our wonderful resources, of the richness of the fields, lands and mines. We believe that we are potentially richer than even the United States. They have depleted many of their precious minerals whereas ours have as yet hardly been scratched. We know that we have even more varied resources than the United States. In spite of this, Mr. Speaker, we are wilfully wasting one of our most precious resources. I speak of water. We know that the water level in many parts of Canada is becoming very low and thereby creating a serious situation. A study of the question has been made by the select committee on conservation of the Ontario legislature. They found some very informative facts from their observations. We know that one-half of the people of Ontario are dependent upon sub-surface water.
Farmers complain that their wells are going dry. In order to secure sufficient water supplies in some areas of Ontario we find that it is necessary to dig deep wells in order to obtain water. In doing that they are robbing adjoining farm wells of necessary water. This problem is not peculiar to Ontario. The hon. member for Regina City (Mr. McCusker) spoke in the house the other night when he so ably brought to the attention of the government the need for the development of the South Saskatchewan river project. He told of how in past days this country, which should have been left for grazing, was put to other agricultural uses, and as a result people cannot live in that area today. I believe that this matter is also of concern to other parts of Canada. I have just learned today of the passing of the dear mother of the hon. member for Regina City, and I am sure that all hon. members would wish to extend to him their sincere sympathy in the loss of this dear one.
The cause of failing ground supplies of water is not hard to find. It means that we

have cleared too much land, that we have cleared swamps which should never have been cleared, and as a result these areas do not act as reservoirs for the storage of water. It is true that the drainage of some swamps has been of great agricultural benefit to the people of Ontario, but in other cases the drainage of swamps has served no useful purpose. What steps can we take to improve the situation? I believe we should have a planned program for increased reforestation. I believe that people should be taught more about this matter. I know that in the county of Northumberland wells which formerly were full of water all year now go dry in the summertime. That is true of many parts of Ontario.
Therefore we must educate our people as to what they can do to preserve the water supply in Ontario. I was pleased to see in the paper today that near Newmarket they are having discussions about how to conserve the water in the Holland river area. We can construct large reservoirs in the river valleys so that these areas will not only serve as a means of flood control but will also serve a very useful purpose so far as safeguarding our water supply is concerned. We should also construct dams on many of our smaller streams wherever that is deemed advisable. I believe the development of electricity in Ontario, and in fact in all parts of Canada, has had a bad effect on water levels. Hon. members will recall that some years ago, before the development of electricity, all our industries were situated on small streams near dams. They derived their power from the dammed-up water, and at the same time the holding back of the water served the very useful purpose of aiding our water supply. I would therefore urge the federal government, through the Department of Resources and Development, to take the lead in devising a useful program for the conservation of water wherever that is necessary. Conservation of our water supply and prevention of soil erosion are inseparable, and through a study of the water supply program much can be done to prevent soil erosion.
These are but a few of the problems confronting us in Canada today. There are many more that will require our wisdom, our confidence and our courage. But I believe that in Canada we have those resources, both material and in the quality of our people, and I have no fear for the future of this country.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Liberal frontbenchers and nearfrontbenchers must grow tired of hearing their praises sung continually by Liberal backbenchers, so perhaps a little honest criticism
The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy for a change might prove somewhat refreshing. I have stated in this house on previous occasions that in my opinion this is no longer a Liberal government; that this government has been persistently departing from many of the basic principles of Liberalism, and is well on the way to establishing the reputation of being one of the most reactionary governments this country has seen for many years. The budget we are discussing at this time confirms that opinion. Through the centuries one of the basic principles of Liberalism as far as taxation is concerned has been that taxes should be levied according to the ability to pay. There was a time when Liberal governments observed that principle in their budgets, but it has been completely disregarded in the measures for raising additional taxes contained in the budget now before us. There is just no regard whatever, in the application of new taxes, to the principle of taxation according to ability to pay.
In the first place the sales tax is increased by 25 per cent right across the board. The small wage earner with a family to support, who notwithstanding the explanation given by the minister must spend anywhere up to 30 per cent of his income on clothing, home furnishings, drugs and a variety of other articles coming within the scope of the sales tax, will pay exactly the same rate of tax as the millionaire. Already in this debate it has been shown that this tax will not be a mere 10 per cent on the retail price of goods but in some cases will amount to as much as 20 or 30 per cent when wholesalers, jobbers and retailers have pyramided their mark-ups. In this increase in the sales tax there is just no recognition of the principle of taxation according to ability to pay. This tax can only drive the cost of living still higher, and will bear hardest on those least able to pay.
In the second place the new levy of 15 per cent on refrigerators, stoves and washing machines will bear particularly heavily on young couples just establishing themselves in homes of their own. The young couple going out to buy their first refrigerator will pay exactly the same rate of taxation as the millionaire who goes out to buy an extra refrigerator for his cellar. Again this tax will bear most severely on those in the lower income brackets. Particularly will that be so in the many cases where the wife has to go to work in order to supplement her husband's income, because she will need these labour saving devices in order to cope with her household duties and at the same time carry a full-time job. In many thousands of homes

The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy today the income of the husband is not sufficient to meet the high cost of living, and that income must of necessity be augmented by the wife's earnings.
In the third place the new surtax on personal income is applied right across the board on incomes of more than $1,000 for single people and $2,000 for married people. In the light of present living costs I suggest that if the minister had not disregarded the principle of taxation according to ability to pay he would have increased the exemptions, before imposing the surtax, to at least $1,500 and $3,000 for single and married people respectively. Had he wanted more taxes from this source, and had he kept ability to pay in mind, he would have increased the surtax in the higher brackets.
In contrast with the taxes I have mentioned we find the minister unduly solicitous of the welfare of corporations. In the first place the corporation tax is to be adjusted so it will not reduce the return on investment below 5 per cent. A new principle of placing a floor on returns from investments before taxation-

speechtext: After taxes.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-was introduced to safeguard corporation profits. In the second place the surtax is not to apply to corporations showing a profit of $10,000 or less. In the third place, while the sales tax is increased by 25 per cent, the surtax on corporations showing net profit of more than $10,000 is only 20 per cent. In the imposition of these new taxes the minister must have been following the injunction that "to him that hath shall be given, and from him that hath not shall be taken away, even that which he hath." The fact of the matter is that government policy as revealed in this budget shows much more concern for the welfare of corporations than for the rank and file of Canadian citizens. In this budget the voice is the voice of the St. James streets of Canada, and not the voice of the ordinary small James streets of the country.
Among other things the amendment of the official opposition regrets the failure of the government to take effective steps to deal with profiteering. Certainly the official opposition and others on this side are not the only ones in Canada who believe there is profiteering at this time which should be curbed. The most recent Gallup poll, published in the Montreal Star of April 14, asked this question: "Do you think there is much profiteering, that is unfair profitmaking, going on in Canada now?" The vote was yes, 75 per cent, and no, 13 per cent. Among the occupational groups, business and
[Mr. Noseworthy. 1
professional men voted 65 per cent yes, and 23 per cent no. The white-collar class voted 75 per cent yes, and only 14 per cent no. Labour voted 79 per cent yes, and only 9 per cent no. Farmers voted 80 per cent yes, and 9 per cent no. The difference between those percentages and 100 per cent represents those who were undecided. The most interesting feature of this Gallup poll is that of those who would vote C.C.F., 85 per cent thought there was profiteering taking place in Canada today, and among those who would vote for the two private enterprise parties, either Liberals or Conservatives, there were 75 per cent who thought there was profiteering taking place. Whether the government believes there is profiteering or not, whether the government believes that some effective measures should be taken to curb profiteering, those of us in the opposition have a great deal of support throughout the country for the belief that there is profiteering.
Surely if the minister had any intention of dealing effectively with profiteering, he would have imposed a more steeply graded corporation tax. In fact many of us believe that a greater degree of equality of sacrifice in the defence effort would be achieved by the imposition of an excess profits tax. The present Minister of Finance speaks with considerable disdain of such a tax. He uses as his argument that such a tax leads to waste and extravagance in production. I do not believe, Mr. Speaker, that is very complimentary to industry in this country. This argument was not used by the government against the excess profits tax during the years of the last war, nor did the tax appear to impede production. During those years the industrialists of Canada gave us the greatest increase in production in our history, notwithstanding the excess profits taxes collected by the government. Let me remind the minister, who apparently had some difficulty in finding ways and means of raising an extra $300 million or $400 million, that since 1941 the government has collected the following amounts in excess profits taxes: 1941-42, $135,168,000-I am giving the figure in fairly round numbers

in 1942-43, $454,581,000;	1943-44,	$468,718,000;	1944-45,
$465,805,000; 1945-46, $494,196,000; 1946-47, $448,698,000; and in 1947-48, although the tax came off in December, 1947 the government collected $227,030,000. The total during those years amounted to $2,694,196,000. I notice, incidentally, that although the excess profits tax was repealed in December, 1947, the government is still collecting back debts on account of excess profits taxes. In the table given on page 64 of the appendix to Hansard of April 10 of this year, it is

estimated that in the fiscal year 1950-51 the government will collect another $10 million on account of excess profits taxes. For five consecutive years the government collected each year between $400 million and $500 million of excess profits taxes.
In those years the minister of finance did not speak with disdain of this tax as does the present minister. In fact, the present Minister of Finance took a very different attitude towards this tax in 1947 to that which he takes today. When in April, 1947, he was being pressed by the official opposition to repeal the excess profits tax, the minister said, as recorded at page 2558 of Hansard for April 29, 1947:
If business conditions had now returned to normal and we could rely upon the forces of competition and bargaining to keep profits at normal levels, we would be justified in repealing this tax . . .
Then again, in the same paragraph:
If business needed larger profits to encourage and enable it to provide additional employment by greater expenditures, we should repeal the tax forthwith.
Then he went on to say that neither of those conditions existed at that time. The minister then thought profits were still running at abnormally high levels. He said that businessmen were competing more in their efforts to expand their investments quickly than in getting down their costs and keeping down the prices at which they sell their products. In April, 1947, the minister said profits were abnormally high. In that year, 1947, according to a table published in the Montreal Gazette on April 14, 1951, one hundred companies whose fiscal years coincide with the calendar year showed net profits after all charges including taxes had been paid of $338,451,000. According to the same table, these same companies in 1950 showed net profits of $475,255,000, an increase over 1947 of 35 per cent. In other words, these same 100 companies showed 35 per cent more profit in 1950 than they showed in 1947, when the present Minister of Finance told us that profits were still abnormally high and therefore merited the continuation of the excess profits tax. If profits were abnormally high in 1947, surely they were still abnormally high in 1950. In fact, in introducing his deferred depreciation policy, the minister implied that he expected profits to remain abnormally high in 1951 and for some years thereafter.
Again, if business did not need larger profits to make capital investments in order, in turn, to provide more employment in 1947, the same thing holds true in 1951. If as the minister stated in April, 1947, business was then more concerned with making profits than in keeping down the prices of goods, surely that situation also holds true for today.
The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy Indeed, every reason the minister gave in April 1947 for retaining the excess profits tax has much greater force today than it had in 1947. Yet the government shies away from an excess profits tax and prefers instead an increased sales tax on clothing, house furnishings, et cetera, and an excise tax on stoves, refrigerators and washing machines. Instead of an excess profits tax or a more steeply-graded corporation tax, the minister prefers to levy a flat surtax on the incomes of all those whose incomes exceed $1,000 and $2,000. The budget we have before us is far from recognizing the principle of taxation according to ability to pay. In fact, this budget might well be termed a profiteers' budget.
Another feature of the budget, taken in conjunction with this government's fiscal policy, is its effect upon the home and the family. Most of us in this house recognize that the home and the family are two institutions that constitute the bulwark of our way of life. Instead of contributing to tne building of home and family life this government, in my opinion, is persistently following a policy that militates against these institutions. Consider the situation of a young couple today who wish to marry, to buy or to build a home and to raise a family. What assistance or encouragement for following that laudable course is to be found in this budget or in this government's general attitude toward rising prices?
In the first place, the price of every single necessity which that couple must buy to live is today higher than ever before in our history. If those young people look around for a house, they find that the down payment has recently been "upped" by government policy until it is now beyond the capacity of the young couple to meet it. If they are fortunate enough to secure an unfurnished house or apartment for rent, the minister's new tax on stoves and refrigerators has made the purchase of those necessary articles far more difficult. If they turn to instalment buying they find that the down payment has been increased and that the time for paying the balance has been shortened. Their clothing, house furnishings, drugs and numerous other articles have increased in price by reason of the increased sales tax. Their personal income will be further reduced by a surtax.
Just how does the government expect Canadians to become home owners and to raise families under those conditions? At a time when we are spending millions oi dollars on defence to protect ourselves from an enemy who would destroy our way of life, our government, by failing to check

The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy inflation, and by making it increasingly difficult for young Canadians to marry, to acquire homes and to raise families, is undermining at home the very foundation of that way of life that we seek to save from destruction by external enemies.
There is another feature of inflation that has not yet been mentioned in this debate. In addition to the high price that every Canadian citizen must pay for the commodities he buys, every municipal taxpayer this fall will find that his tax bill is increased because of the increased cost of living and because of inflation. The municipality which I represent just last week increased its mill rate by twenty mills. That increase was rendered necessary because of the higher wages and salaries the municipality was called upon to pay to its employees and the increased costs of all the materials that the municipality had to buy in order to service it. Taxpayers and home owners all across Canada, in their municipal tax bills, are finding repercussions of inflation. Those increased taxes have to be charged up to inflation. Unfortunately, municipal governments are not in the happy position of the federal government and the Minister of Finance. From the minister's speech when he introduced his budget and when he announced his surplus of approximately $200 million, one would almost gather that the minister was not particularly disturbed about inflation. Inflation certainly makes it easier to balance budgets and to provide surpluses. I think it is readily admitted that that surplus was directly due to the increased costs, the rise in prices, and with that the rise in profits and the rise in the minister's taxes. Municipal officers are not in that happy position. When they find it necessary to increase the salaries and wages of municipal employees, when they find it necessary to pay more for the goods they buy, they have no recourse but to increase taxes on the home owner, which is one more tax making it still more difficult to maintain homes in this country.
The government's policy on inflation was apparently set forth by the Minister of Finance in his broadcast as reported in the Montreal Gazette of April 18. It says:
Though rationing, price control and wage freezing were useful instruments during the last war, when almost half of our national output was devoted to war, they are not appropriate measures at the present stage when only some 10 per cent is being devoted to defence needs.
Apparently there is no relation between the rising cost of living and the need for those controls. The need for those controls is to be determined, according to government policy, strictly on the basis of the percentage of our

national income that is going into national defence; regardless of the effect of rising prices on the people of this country, no measures will be taken on that ground by this government.
The minister went on to say:
Existing controls on essential materials and the various programs we are following, designed to increase the total savings of the community, should enable us to come through.
We should certainly appreciate hearing from the minister, or from some government speaker, a more detailed account of just what these measures are which are designed to increase the total savings of the community. The only one that I can observe is the possibility of the minister having another $200 million or $300 million surplus at the end of the next fiscal year. I presume that could be considered as community savings. The higher down payments on houses, the higher taxes on stoves, refrigerators and washing machines, the surtax on income, the increased sales tax will probably force many people to buy fewer of the things that they absolutely need; but I fail to see where these measures are likely to increase, in the words of the minister, the total savings of the community.
The government's policy apparently is influenced by that of the United States. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) intimated to us the other night that we were waiting to see how these controls work out in the United States. I notice that in his broadcast the minister has a slight change in the phrasing that he used. Heretofore in this house we have been speaking of price control and wage control. I do not know that we have been particularly considering wage freezing, but the minister speaks of rationing, price control and wage freezing, which, in effect, is exactly the position in regard to controls in the United States.
In its special inflation issue of Sunday, April 1, the New York Times has this to say regarding controls:
The present pattern of controls to deal with the inflationary threat is mixed-soft here, hard there. This is the picture:
As to prices, the controls are on the whole soft.
As to wages, the controls are on the whole hard. A general freeze was imposed on January 26.
As to credit, the controls are on the whole soft.
It is quite evident that the minister, in speaking of price control and wage freezing, is adopting the principle underlying these controls in the United States, and one which the Minister of Trade and Commerce assured us the government is watching very closely before embarking upon any such policy in this country.
I would simply close, Mr. Speaker, in asking just what mandate this government

has for following the example of the United States in a matter so closely affecting the economy and the life of this country as does the cost of living? Since when did this country give any government a mandate to shun matters that were of national importance just because they were difficult? Many of the arguments that we have heard against price control from the government side of the house were simply enumerations of the difficulties that stand in the way of price control. What is true, I submit, Mr. Speaker, is that this government, secure in its overwhelming majority, secure in the fact that there is no immediate general election in the offing, can afford, or thinks it can afford, to ignore the opinion of 75 per cent of the people of this country, to ignore the demands of practically every organized group except possibly chambers of commerce, and carry on without price control. In closing I submit that were this an election year this government would not dare face the people of this country on the policy that they are pursuing at this time.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to be representing the constituency of Fort William in this debate, and in doing so I must express some of the things that have been told to me during the past week or so. Before doing that I should like to pay a tribute to my comrade, friend and good fellow worker here, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. May-bank). We were every-day friends and companions and he did a lot with his sane, common-sense judicial advice to keep me out of difficulties into which I had the knack of getting.
I cannot forget the first time I visited him when I came down here in 1935. You know what new members think of the House of Commons. They think that the men who come down here love money above everything else, but they soon get that knocked out of their heads. When I paid my first call on the hon. member I found him reading Dr. Smith's commentary on "The Minor Prophets". This was the lawyer from Winnipeg, the former alderman and member of the provincial legislature reading "The Minor Prophets" under the leadership of Dr. Smith.
I looked at him and I suppose I showed some surprise because he said, "What is the matter?" I said, "I am agreeably surprised
The Budget-Mr. Mclvor but I know you will get there just the thing you need for anything in life. From Amos you will get the idea of justice and how to dispense it. From Hosea you will get the meaning of real love and the source from which it comes. From Daniel the prophet you will get the way of courage and strength to meet any lion you may meet on the way." The hon. member was independent, but he had a judicial mind. He was kind and courteous and, like myself, enjoyed a good clean joke. I never heard a joke from him that I could not repeat to my grandchildren.
Coming to the budget, may I say that I think that it is a great budget. Like many great things, there are things in it that need to be improved. That shows it is a budget of growth. Some people in Fort William during the past weeks have objected to every tax there is. Nobody likes to pay taxes. I do not like to pay taxes. The only way I like to pay them is when I can pay them without knowing, but I do not like it when I have to hand out ready cash because it is difficult to hold on to cash.
I have five letters objecting vigorously to those hidden taxes and to the idea that the British North America Act be amended to allow the provinces to impose a three per cent retail tax. These letters are all from Fort William and I shall give the names of the writers because I do not think they have any business writing me unless they want to back up what they say and let their names appear on Hansard. These men are all businessmen and they say that the small businessman will be put out of business. One letter is from a man who has lost both legs. He is well known in Fort William and he says that he cannot carry on. I have letters from Gerry Hardware, Strachan Jewelry store, Mahon Electric and Clemens grocery. These are all outstanding businessmen and they object vigorously to these taxes. I hope it is not too late for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) to change his mind.
Another matter to which there is objection is the change in the postal procedure in order to save money. I do not think the postage on books should be increased. Our public library sends books out to people in the country who are not able to enjoy the modern conveniences we have. Some of these people have battery radios which have the knack of running down, but when they get one or half a dozen books from the library it is a great treat to them. I think the government would be well advised to go back to the former rate and allow these people out in the country to enjoy their reading.
I must say that I do not have one objection to the taxes on cigarettes and tobacco. The

The Budget-Mr. Mclvor hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruick-shank) objected, not to the tax on cigarettes but to there being no tax on liquor. Another man writes to me and says that the post office should attempt to increase their revenues in some other manner. I suggest to the minister that he limit our franking privileges to letters only, and not have it cover the magazines we send out. If we had to pay for the magazines we send out we would be more careful what we sent. I do not know how many hon. members will agree with me on that. If we say that the revenue should be raised then let us impose the taxes some other place because we are told in the budget that the Minister of Finance has to raise certain taxes. Where is he going to get them? The budget is his plan to raise them, and if some of these taxes are to be cancelled let us put others in their place. Another man said to me: Reduce the tax on utilities of the home and impose an extra tax on beer and liquor.

Before any increase is made in the amount of $40 a month paid to old age pensioners 1 would say that every cripple in Canada, every man who has to use a wheel chair and is not able to get around, should be paid1 $40 a month. Of course, Mr. Speaker, a little drink does not hurt. I have been interested in athletics all my life and still am, but there are certain things in the athletic world that give me some concern. The way we can help our tax situation and the Minister of Finance is by the development of our natural resources. I have noticed that nickel is now being rationed. In our district we have perhaps

one of the greatest sources of nickel in Canada. The International Nickel Company-bought up all the claims that looked good but that is all that happened. I know that the budget will be hard on those who like to spend their own money. An increase of 20 per cent in income tax is pretty heavy but, as I said before, we have asked our minister to raise these taxes, and I think that is one of the most popular sources from which to get the money. We must raise these taxes. The other reason that we have for supporting the budget is that there may be something in it that will help to stop inflation.
I should like to say a word about Korea. It is dangerous for an Irishman to take sides but I should like to pay my tribute to President Truman for his courage. He was in a terrible corner, showed his courage, and I admire him for it. I also admire General MacArthur as an outstanding soldier and perhaps a part statesman.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Go on, give him a clap.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

I have just received a note and it indicates to me the greatness of this House of Commons. It says that the Maple Leafs are going to win the Stanley cup. I did not know there were such outstanding prophets in this house. They may be wrong this time. Both President Truman _ and General MacArthur are outstanding citizens. I think the best thing for us to do is to let them fight their own battles. I think you will find before the battle is over these two men will come together. Just as one hon. member said today, we do not stand for any appeasement. I think of some of the letters I have received during the last three weeks from communist people who say they want peace. I have answered each of those letters, and have said they should put at the top of their program the abolition of the iron curtain. They should let the workers of Russia see what is going on in the outside world, as they cannot see now, and let the workers outside see what is going on in Russia; then there will be more chance of their coming together. But I repeat that I
The Budget-Mr. Pearkes am not a bit afraid of Russia or China, because sooner or later any country that treats God as a myth will go to the bowwows.
I want to mention just two other matters. In Fort William we have difficulties in connection with floods. For certain reasons the river there is flooding more extensively every year. I must pay my tribute to the deputy minister of public works, whom I interviewed today; and I was pretty stiff about it. He gave me every encouragement that the dominion government would do the fair thing by the province and the city. I did not bother the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier), but I am sure he will be even more generous.
Fort William has been very pleased with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier). During the past summer he said that if the St. Lawrence waterway was not developed in co-operation with the United States, Canada would go ahead and do it herself. That might be a splendid stimulant to wake up the people of the United States. I think it would be a great thing for the world if this development could be accomplished, and I can assure the minister he will get every co-operation from us.
I should like to speak for an hour, Mr. Speaker, but I know it is not the men who speak longest who say the most. As a boy I chose Canada as the land of my adoption, and I have never been sorry. It is the greatest country on earth. We could boast about the things we have. We have the greatest wheat fields on earth, the longest railway in the world, the best machinery for handling wheat. We also have the best young men and maidens the world knows, as they have proved in the past. When we think of Canada there is music in the name. We feel like the Irishman who said the real patriot was the man who was loyal to his native land, whether or not he was born there. We are loyal to Canada because we believe it is the land of the free, a place where we can grow and develop and train our children according to the way we have been led. We will lead them Godward, and Canada toward the eternal kingdom.

Like the hon. member I do not smoke cigarettes, but unlike him I do enjoy my little toddy. It was with a little disappointment I noticed that when the hon. member was passing around his numerous bouquets, and particularly when he was referring to the great game of hockey, he
2194	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Pearkes overlooked the fact that there is a team from a little town called Nanaimo, where the most westerly of all hockey rinks in Canada is located. The team travelled all the way from the other side of British Columbia to northwestern Ontario to play Fort Frances in the Allan cup playdowns; and the series is tied at one game each. I know Fort Frances is not in my hon. friend's constituency, but it is very close to it; and I was a little disappointed that he did not hand a bouquet to that hockey team from far off. However, I must say that the Fort Frances team played an exceedingly good game and the Nanaimo team learned much from them.
I feel that many advantages arise from the fact that we have an Easter recess which enables hon. members to visit their constituencies and obtain the opinions of their people in regard to what is being done in this parliament. I believe the advantage is greater the further the constituency is from this capital city. I took advantage of the recess to visit my constituency on Vancouver island, and in moving around among the people I found their interest was focused on the then and still rising cost of living and the inflationary trends prevalent in British Columbia. When the budget was brought down I think the first reaction was that the increased taxation was not as heavy as had been expected. Mr. Speaker, discussion of the budget and its various provisions and implications may well be regarded as a general survey of the national economy and an examination of the state of the country. Speeches delivered so far by almost all opposition members have revealed a definite pattern, that pattern taking the form of a concerted attack on the budget. The criticisms have been notable for their lack of constructive suggestions. A dispassionate onlooker would gather the impression that the main purpose of the critics is to tear down the budgetary structure rather than consolidate its foundations. Parliament, composed as it is of representatives of all parties, both government and opposition members, is presumed to be the mirror of the nation. Keeping this thought in mind, one may well inquire at this stage, what substantial segment of the country do the criticisms voiced so far represent? It is extremely difficult to reconcile these criticisms with the seemingly general acceptance of the budget by the country at large.
Some suggestions have been made as to the taxation measures that should be discarded and the fiscal policies that should be made effective to provide the necessary revenues for the management of the country's affairs. Too many criticisms have been notable for their lack of realism and objectivity.

Canada's taxation structure is at best a delicate fabric. It must be designed to establish a proper balance between the national economy and the economy of the ten provinces constituting the dominion. An ill-conceived national taxation policy can, by reason of its implications and repercussions, so operate as to deprive the provinces of essential revenues. Overly heavy taxation of spirituous liquors is a case in point.
No government, federal or provincial, relishes the task of increasing the burden of taxation. But there are times when a state of national or near national emergency leaves no other course open to the government. Such a situation now confronts the government of Canada. My deeply respected and able leader, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), recently expressed his views in this respect when addressing a group of students of the Hawkesbury high school who visited the parliament buildings. He emphasized that national necessity imposed on the government unpleasant duties, such as the levying of taxes to provide revenues for the purchase of death-dealing armaments and the waging of war against the forces whose sole aim is the destruction of our civilization and all that it implies in the realm of human rights and fundamental liberties. The action which the government has taken on behalf of the people of Canada is actuated by but one desire, the determination to prevent occurrences such as the rape of Korea and the further enslavement of the free peoples of the world.
A nation is no stronger than the sum total of its individual strength. In this time of crisis, the people living in the 262 ridings that make up the dominion must so integrate their efforts as to give the fullest support to the government in the pursuit of its main policy, that of strengthening the country from within and helping friendly and still free nations meet the threat of the common enemy, Soviet Russia and its satellites.
My constituency, Prescott county, is in the happy position of being able to make a not inconsequential contribution to the national effort. But Prescott county's contribution is conditioned on co-operation. During the second world war my riding, where the topography of the land is admirably suited for aviation purposes, had the benefit of two airfields, one situated at Pendleton and the other at St. Eugene. These two airfields, which played an important part in the expansion and full development of the eminently successful commonwealth air training plan, have been virtually unused since 1945. A moderate outlay would be sufficient to ensure their rehabilitation and utilization. Hawkes-
The Budget-Mr. Bruneau bury has a flying club which has been in existence for several years now. The unflagging enthusiasm of its members has ensured its successful operation in spite of many handicaps, among others the lack of finances. The preliminary training of fliers under the direction of flying clubs like the one operating on the outskirts of Hawkesbury is directly associated with the broad pattern of national defence. Young aviation enthusiasts learn the fundamentals of flying at these clubs. The theoretical and practical knowledge of flying acquired at these clubs constitutes an important preliminary step in any national air training plan. Bearing in mind the over-all cost of training each flier, the national budget is relieved of a portion of the financial burden the complete air training course entails. I have been urging for some time now the installation of a beacon at the airfield of the Hawkesbury flying club. Such a beacon would be of great help to the flying enthusiasts who, by reason of their employment, can only engage in night flying. The benefits to be derived from the installation of a beacon are so obvious that I need not labour the point. The very small outlay required would pay dividends to this country.
I should like to stress another factor that ties in closely with the national defence program. I have in mind the decentralization of industry. Economic and strategic reasons make such a decentralization increasingly imperative. Decentralization relieves transportation congestion in heavily populated areas and facilitates the quick movement of traffic both in times of peace and war. New methods of warfare centred around the use of the atomic bomb and its more lethal companion, the hydrogen bomb, are undoubtedly the most compelling reason for the decentralization of industry. Prescott county, situated as it is midway between Ottawa and Montreal, is splendidly located to meet the needs of decentralization. There is ample power for the operation of almost any type of industry, and the county is well endowed with rail and highway transportation facilities.
The full development of Canada's agricultural possibilities is another paramount consideration. This country is most fortunate in that there is a fairly happy balance between its agriculture and its industry. We are well aware of the outstanding part Canada's agriculture played in the successful prosecution of two world wars. I fully endorse the action taken by the government, and confirmed by a parliamentary majority,

The Budget-Mr. Bruneau in connection with the voting of a $65 million subsidy to the western wheat growers. However, I will avail myself of the opportunity presented by the reference to this matter to emphasize once again the importance of maintaining a proper relationship between all the constituent elements of our agricultural economy. There is an all too pronounced tendency in some quarters, and among some informed and less informed citizens, to regard the farmers of the eastern section of the country as quite capable of coping with their own problems. There is such a thing as penalizing farmers for their qualities of sturdy individualism. I have often asked myself if eastern farmers receive all the encouragement to which their efforts and initiative entitle them. I strongly urge the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to do his utmost to ensure the setting of a floor price for butter at 62 cents a pound, as suggested by Mr. A. L. Sloan, secretary of the Prescott and Russell counties federation of agriculture, and Mr. Emile Laplante, president general de 1'union des cultivateurs franco-ontariens. In relation to its farming population, Prescott county is the largest producing centre of cheddar cheese in North America. Flax is grown in large quantities.
Another drawback for the eastern farmers is the rampaging Nation river, the wickedest river in Canada which at flood times creates havoc on a vast area of the fertile golden triangle of the Ottawa valley. I sincerely hope that before too long a program will be devised to check this stream.
A full defence effort should not divert attention from the pressing needs of many of our fellow-Canadians. I have in mind the aged people of this country who have reached the twilight stage of life and are incapable of fending for themselves or providing for their own sustenance. There is too the tragic case of invalids who know not where to turn for succour, and who have no kith or kin to lend them a helping hand along life's all too thorny path.
There is some evidence that the program of price stabilization applied in the United States is producing results which should be reflected in the Canadian economy. Canadians are following this economic experiment with interest.
Taken by and large, the 1951 budget is one that should not fail to commend itself to the people of this country. It will be assayed and judged in terms of its ultimate results. Those results will, I feel confident, help most substantially in the furtherance of Canada's national defence program and redound also to the ultimate benefit of the Canadian population.
IMr. Bruneau.]
