Mr. Speaker, there are a few matters pertaining to my own province which I should like to bring to the attention of the house this evening. Before doing so I have a few observations to make concerning the budget. The first is with regard to the depreciation allowance the minister announced in his budget this year. Ever since income tax and corporation tax have come to be a major source of revenue they have always been allowed corporation depreciation rates levied on a very prudent, proven and well established basis. I believe it is a great mistake to depart from this procedure. I realize that there is a shortage of metals and steel that go into the making of machines, or in other words, capital goods. It was the minister's intention to discourage the buying of capital goods through the adoption of these new rates of depreciation. It would seem to me to have been much better to adopt a system of priorities such as that established during the last war. Then, if anyone wants to buy a new machine or spend a large amount of money on capital goods, he has to get a permit from the minister before he can proceed. It seems to me that would have been a much better system than the one proposed by the minister in the budget.
The second matter to which I want to refer is the tobacco tax. Cigarettes and tobacco do not greatly concern me, and I am not one to encourage their use. It is a sort of dirty habit, but today one cannot class cigarettes and tobacco as a luxury. They are used by many of our people, and it seems to me a lot of money to have to put out forty cents for twenty cigarettes. It seems still more foolish to me when you cross to the United States and buy cigarettes for around twenty cents, but when you come back into Canada you have to pay forty cents. It does seem to me that the spread is too great, and perhaps we have gone too far in the taxation of tobacco and cigarettes. The tax was steep enough before this increase was brought down.
The third matter I wish to bring to the attention of the house concerns the sales tax, I should say the increase in the sales tax. Personally, I am against sales taxes in any way, shape or form. I do believe that if we have to have a sales tax the amount of the tax should be shown to the people buying a shirt or a pair of shoes. I realize that this is poor politics, but I am certainly against any hidden taxes whatever. If we have to have a sales tax, I believe the amount of it should be shown in the cost of the goods to the buyer. I go still further and say that the sales tax is a bad tax. It bears hardest on

those who can least afford to pay it. I have heard it said by some officers in the Department of Finance that the sales tax is not pyramided. I cannot agree with that, Mr. Speaker. Anyone who is familiar with the retail trade in this country knows that the sales tax is pyramided to quite an extent. The retail mark-up is always taken on the sales tax as well as on the actual cost of the goods to the merchant. As to automobiles, I will admit that I do not believe there is a mark-up on the sales tax; but as far as I know, that is one of the few things that do not bear a sales tax mark-up on the retail price.
As I say, it is a hard tax on a great many people and is one that I certainly would like to see done away with. But if we must have a sales tax, I am all for showing it on the actual cost of the article to the purchaser at the retail level, or for working out some system whereby this may be done, because I think it should be brought home to the people at all times how much it costs to run this country, so that they will have a greater interest in that matter at all times.
Now I shall come a little closer to home. I should like to bring to the attention of the house this evening the matter of freight rates. To the maritime provinces this is a matter of great importance. Unless some better system can be worked out with regard to freight rates, we in the maritime provinces are certainly not going to have too much prosperity. We in the maritime provinces are so situated that our natural market in which to trade is not east and west but north and south, namely, in the New England states and the state of New York. But if we are closed off from those markets, or if we have to trade with western Canada and central Canada, certainly some system must be worked out whereby the freight rates will not bear so heavily on us in the maritimes.
I know that is an extremely difficult question. It is a hard one to work out. In the past efforts have been made to rectify that situation, and they have helped. But with the great increase in freight rates that has taken place over these last two years, it has become a much more difficult question to us in the maritimes than ever before. We had a great deal of prosperity during the war and since, and perhaps, with the great defence program getting under way again, we may not feel these heavy freight rates in the maritimes as much as we would if we were in ordinary times; but I can assure everyone that if the maritime provinces are to be prosperous, some cheaper method must be
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield worked out by which they can trade with the central provinces and also with western Canada.
I should also like to commend to the minister the continuation of the subsidy on feed grains. I can assure the minister that this subsidy is a great help to the farmers in our part of the world. It also helps to keep down the price of milk and other dairy products. I also think that it is a good thing for the western farmers, as it helps them to dispose of a great deal of their coarse grain. They can really grow those coarse grains in the western country much more cheaply and of much better quality than we can in the maritimes. I would strongly urge the Minister of Finance that the subsidy on these feed grains be retained; and I am sure that consideration of this suggestion would be greatly appreciated by all the farmers not only in the maritimes but in Quebec and Ontario as well.
It is perhaps a dangerous thing to raise this question of coal, inasmuch as people from the maritime provinces have been talking about coal for a long time; but a large item in the economic life of Nova Scotia is that commodity known as black coal. Today it is having a hard run against oil, in all its forms, that is burnt today not only in Ontario and Quebec but even in the maritime provinces themselves. There is, however, a large market for coal here in Ontario. Our coal now comes up to Montreal but little of it passes beyond that point or reaches Ontario. I notice that the number of tons of coal mined in Nova Scotia and in Alberta was less this year than it was a year ago but that the importations of United States coal have been greater.
I should like to see adopted some national policy with regard to coal, to the end that more of our Nova Scotia coal as well as Alberta coal would be brought to the Ontario market, thus giving the miners in our province more work. In addition, perhaps a greater number of mines could be operated than there are at present. There is no doubt about it that in our part of the country not nearly as many coal mines are in operation today as there used to be. Alberta, of course, has all kinds of resources, but we in Nova Scotia are not so fortunate. It would be a great gesture on the part of the rest of the country if some kind of national fuel policy could be drawn up with regard to coal, as a result of which more of our Nova Scotia coal might be brought to Ontario.
There is another way in which I am sure the government could greatly assist the people in Nova Scotia and in New Brunswick. That is by the establishing of more

The Budget-Mr. Stanfield industries in connection with this great program of national defence that this government has just undertaken. If they could not locate large plants down there, perhaps a large number of small plants could be established in the various cities and towns throughout those two provinces, in which subcontracting work could be carried on. I do not know whether or not the same thing could be worked out with regard to Newfoundland, but I presume that a certain amount could be done over there. But I feel certain that, if the government so desired, a great deal of new employment could be provided in the maritime provinces by bringing to these provinces many of the industries that I feel they are contemplating setting up in Ontario and Quebec. I think it is only fair that those industries should be spread around the country as much as possible.
In Nova Scotia and in New Brunswick we have not the same full employment that is enjoyed in Ontario and Quebec. I am sure that the establishing of some of these plants in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick would greatly improve the employment situation in that part of the country. It would also perhaps have the effect of permanently building up many more industries down in . those two provinces. I hope that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) will listen to those of us on this side of the house who have been urging this course of action for some time. The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) and the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) have been continually pounding on this question. I certainly give them my wholehearted support in the good work that they have been doing, and I do hope that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) will do something about it.
Hon. members will recall, Mr. Speaker, that when the Cuban market was open to us in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick it was a great market for many of the products of the maritime provinces. A few years ago the Liberal government brought in the West Indies trade treaty. The Cuban government took exception to it, and they stopped buying anything, or practically anything, from us in Canada. At that time we lost some of the best markets we had for our fish, potatoes and many other products, and we have never obtained a market to take the place of the Cuban market.
The West Indies market is a small market so far as we are concerned. I should like to see the Minister of Trade and Commerce take steps to try to get the Cuban market back for our exports in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. I am not saying that the West

Indies trade treaty was a bad one, or anything of that kind, but it was a very tough one for the people in the maritimes. The West Indies market in no way, shape or form took the place of the Cuban market.
The English market is another market that we in the maritimes really must have. I do regret that there has been a little-I do not know the word to use-disagreement or misunderstanding between the English and ourselves with regard to exports. We had enjoyed the English market for many, many years, and up until the second world war broke out. We all know since that time England was not in a position to trade with us so freely or to put up good money for the exports from our country which had to be paid for in dollars. The result was that we lost our apple industry. We also lost a great deal of the lumber market, and other markets that we enjoyed, such as markets for pit props and other things which we sold to the British isles for so many years previous to 1940. It was another hard blow for- us in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, perhaps more so to New Brunswick than to Nova Scotia. However, I am glad to learn that the English market for our pit props has been reopened to us since the first of 1951.
When the government is working out trade agreements with the British isles I do hope that they will not overlook us, but will try to get our apple market back for us, and also the market for our long lumber, and many other of our commodities which we had enjoyed over there so many years prior to the second world war.
The English people are among the best there is. They always pay their bills, and we should make every effort to get back with them all the markets that we have lost.
If the minister has any great amount of money to throw around, to play Santa Claus with, as he sometimes has, perhaps he could appropriate a little to the maritime provinces to help conserve the forests of those provinces. The forest wealth of the maritime provinces is the greatest form of wealth we have. It has fast disappeared in the last few years. I should like to see something worked out whereby our forests could be conserved in the same way as they are being conserved in Sweden, in Finland and in many other European countries, where they have been successful in having large timber cuts each year, but have also been able to conserve their forest wealth.
The forest wealth is of very great importance to us, and I do not hear a great deal about it in this house. It is a matter of great concern to us in the maritime provinces.

Every hon. member should take a greater interest in conserving the forest wealth of this country.
Perhaps the house has listened long enough to what I have to say; but I do wish to say that we in the maritime provinces, as everybody knows, are not as fortunate as the people in western Canada. I do ask you all to give the very best consideration to our requests and to the special needs and the special help that we need in those provinces.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since listening to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) deliver his budget, I have been somewhat indisposed, but I managed to pull myself together tonight in order to make a few comments on the budget because of the importance of this matter to my constituents, and because in the time that has elapsed since he gave his budget speech and now I have received communications from a number of people.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, before proceeding, that for one in my condition I do not get very much inspiration from the rather bored expression on the face of the Minister of Finance, but I do get some inspiration from the enlightened attention I am receiving from the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson), so I shall continue with that inspiration.
We in this group fully realize that the Minister of Finance must have the funds to give effect to the decisions of this parliament -there is no question about that. And we know that money has to be raised and we know you cannot raise taxes without taking something away from people. This group believes in the principles of arithmetic, that two and two always make four, but we want to be sure that you take the two from the right people. We criticize this budget, Mr. Speaker, on two grounds. The first is, there is no specific provision in the budget for the checking of inflation.
I understand the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) told a group of labour people representing the Canadian Congress of Labour, the Trades and Labour Congress and the Catholic Federation of Labour that the government did not see fit to introduce price controls and subsidies now, but that when the budget was introduced they would find that it contained some provisions for checking inflation. Well, I am quite sure, Mr. Speaker, that a great number of members in this house and a great number of people in the country are not satisfied that this budget is a determined effort to check inflation.
We in this group believe, Mr. Speaker, in income tax as a fair and a sound tax, and we 80709-142
The Budget-Mr. Herridge believe in the principle of taxation on the basis of ability to pay. We do not believe that this budget, in these serious and urgent times, has been drafted sufficiently on the principle of ability to pay.
I am not going to speak at length this evening. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) gave a very full criticism of the budget. We had an excellent speech from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), particularly that portion of his speech in which he dealt with possibilities for changes in the act in connection with deduction of medical dues and so on. Then we had a very down to earth oration from the well loved member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). This afternoon the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) gave what I thought was an excellent criticism of the budget based on soundly presented evidence. I am going to deal with just a few items in the budget. I shall stay with the budget entirely from my point of view.
My constituents are already informing me that they consider this 25 per cent increase in the sales tax, the increase from 8 to 10 per cent, entirely wrong, and I think they are correct. We in this group are very much opposed to the principle of sales taxes and hidden taxes because we believe they are oppressive and unfair. This sales tax pyramids because it is applied by the manufacturer, by the wholesaler and by the retailer. We believe that this type of tax is not sound in principle, and if the government see fit to apply it, it should be applied at the retailer's level so that the consuming public will be asked to pay the 10 per cent only once.
The new 15 per cent levy on refrigerators, washing machines, gas and electric stoves was quite a surprise to many people in this country. We believe that that tax could have been omitted from the budget. This group particularly, and many members of this house, realize that the basis of the Canadian economy, if it is to be a stable and worthwhile economy, is the building of satisfactory homes. We believe that this tax is going to work considerable hardship on people, particularly young people who are attempting to furnish new home units and things of that sort.
The increase in the cigarette tax of three cents a package will create a small hardship for a good number of Canadians, but I do not think we can complain too much about that under the circumstances. While I am one of those who enjoy the so-called filthy habit of smoking pipe tobacco, I do not think we are suffering too much in the increase
2208	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Herridge in the tax on tobacco from 67 cents to $1.15 a pound. These are not essentials. I have found from experience, and as a result of my wife's prodding, that on occasion I can do without these things when I am pushed. So in future I shall be allowed just that much less tobacco and my budget for tobacco will be the same.
The increase in the special excise tax from 15 to 25 per cent on cars, radios and luxuries is one that we could expect. We cannot complain about the tax being increased on luxuries. I do not know whether we can complain too much about the increase in the tax on radios. But there are certain people in this country, particularly those with lower incomes and who may require a car with which to travel to work, or who would like to enjoy a radio, who may find this somewhat of a hardship.
I come now to the 20 per cent defence levy on personal income taxes, effective July 1. We contend that there should have been higher exemptions from that tax; that it should not have been a flat 20 per cent, that it should have been graduated. It will bear heavily on a certain group of people in this country, but if the exemptions for this special levy had been raised to $1,500 and $3,000 this defence levy could have been more easily borne by the majority of the Canadian people.
We in this group are pleased to note that the government has seen fit to allow union and professional dues to be deducted for income tax purposes. I think that is a tribute to the efforts of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), which were supplemented by the efforts of this group. I remember the time when that was first brought up and there was so little support. It was considered to be a sort of Utopian idea; it was considered to be unnecessary. I am glad to note that the government of the day has seen fit to recognize the constructive and progressive work of the C.C.F. group in this house.
I understand1 that the corporation taxes under this budget will impose a tax of about 50 per cent on the profits of a corporation making over $10,000 per year. Under normal conditions that would be considered quite a high rate of taxation. I understand that the smaller corporations making a profit of $10,000 or less will not be affected by an increase in taxation. I am not so sure but that the smaller companies could have stood at least a 5 per cent increase from 15 per cent to 20 per cent. Some of the smaller companies are operated by people who draw good salaries and they are permitted to make a profit up to $10,000. When you consider 

The Budget-Mr. Herridge
I know it is difficult. We have wide spaces to travel in Canada, but I suggest that the government would be well advised to have more spot check audits in various types of businesses and for certain individuals. When we come to the question of taxation we must realize that the only persons who are bound to pay their full tax are the wage and salaried workers who have their tax deducted at the source, and the farmers who are selling their products through marketing agencies such as the wheat pool, Tree Fruits Limited in British Columbia, vegetable growers organizations, dairy co-operatives, and so on. I am not suggesting that there are large numbers of dishonest people, but the ones to whom I have referred are the only people concerning whom the government can be certain that they are collecting every dollar of income tax owing to the government. They are placed in a somewhat different position from any other people in this country.
The question of taxation in modern times has reached astounding proportions. I want to indicate the position of the average man of modest income in a province like British Columbia under the present circumstances. I want to indicate the taxes that will be paid by the average home or farm owner. He is not born more than a few minutes before his parents have got to buy a birth certificate so that the Minister of Finance will know he is here. Then he has a land tax, a school tax, and a provincial sales tax in British Columbia. Then he has an electrical energy tax, and a poll tax if he lives in a municipality. All citizens who use automobiles and gasoline pay the gasoline tax. After going along for a while he decides to get married and he has to buy a marriage licence.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Amusement tax.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And there is the amusement tax. I appreciate the assistance of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) very much. Then this person decides to get married and for the first time he begins to realize the full impact of federal taxes. Then he knows what income tax means, the excise taxes, the federal sales tax, and the tariffs which are a form of tax. On top of that he has an insurance tax. I am not giving them all; I am only giving the more important ones. I do not want to discourage people too much, but then he has many licences to buy. He buys a business licence, a radio licence, a fishing licence, a hunting licence, a car licence and a driver's licence. After he has paid taxes all during his life he dies, and then they insist upon his relatives paying for the death certificate so the Minister of Finance will know he is gone. Then shortly


after his death the monument manufacturer comes around and says, "Don't you think it would be nice to put up a nice headstone to your relative?" He might suggest, "I will put on it 'Rest in peace; Abbott cannot get you now.' "
The situation in the world today is serious. The position of Canada, in common with all other members of the United Nations, is very serious. I am disturbed by the business as usual attitude of a good number of corporations and individuals in this country whose main motive in life is still the making of profits. I am not going to be sanctimonious about this. We live in a capitalist society and companies have to make profits in order to exist, just as individuals who invest their money have to make reasonable profits. But I meet any number of people who seem to have no conception of what faces the western world, but are just as keen as ever on raking in every dollar from the Canadian economy that the law will permit, and in many instances more than the law legally allows.
There is evidence of that right in this house, and in the newspapers of the country. Look at the prospectuses being issued by those making application for gas pipe line charters. You should read some of the literature being circulated in the United States. They say that in Canada there is a glorious opportunity to make more money than can be made by any other investment; and it is a highly productive investment. It is the same with the oil pipe lines; you should see some of the prospectuses I have in my office. There is no mention of the seriousness of the situation. And mind you, when you are doing these things, building pipe lines and so on, there are great opportunities for depreciation and things of that kind. Look at my -own province, where the British Columbia Telephone Company is asking for an increase in its authorized capital from $25 million to $75 million. People do not realize that the telephone business is the greatest industry in North America. The owners of the Bell company in the United States have more capital and make more profits than United States Steel and two American railroads put together. This new capital in British Columbia will come principally from the United States; and you see advertisements in Canadian newspapers, even here in Ottawa, in connection with preferred stock issues and bonds which are being sold in the United States. The lure, shall I say, or the whole approach is that here is an opportunity to make more money than usual, more money than average business is able to make.
The same situation exists in connection with other corporations, and again I am

going to mention International Nickel, which I consider one of the vilest monopolies in this country today. These companies think of profits while we are asking men to join the armed forces and defend the principles of the United Nations in Korea. Before I proceed may I say I firmly believe that no member of the active forces who leaves Canada to serve this country in the field should be required to pay income tax on the pay he receives as a member of the armed forces. I think that is the least we can do for them and their dependents while they are overseas. But here we have these large profits, with people going about their business quite unconcerned over the fact that the whole world about them may be crumbling. It takes a great deal to shake large segments of humanity out of their lethargy and greed.
I have suggested that we should have an excess profits tax. This would be a way to assist companies in meeting wage demands, and would help keep prices and wages in better relationship if applied with price controls and subsidies. In addition it would give us the extra money we require to do something about old age pensions, which were dealt with so well the other evening by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). In addition it would make it possible for us to distribute the burden more fairly and lift what we consider an unfair burden from the shoulders of the lower income groups.
In view of my approach to the budget and my criticisms, Mr. Speaker, when the vote is taken I intend to support the subamendment and the amendment.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like other members I have received during the past few days many messages and letters from farmers in my riding asking the government for a floor price on butter, namely 62 cents to the producer. I know this is a slippery matter as a certain party has learned at its expense. However, even if the problem should be a difficult one, that is no reason for refusing to cope with it.
The workers in our cities and villages must be asking themselves how it is that in these critical times, when the cost of living is already so high, public men are seeking to set the price of butter at what must appear a very high level. If it is fair to set a reasonable floor price for the farmer, I believe it is only logical to let workers know the reason why. I should like to give my personal impression on the matter without, of course, attempting to solve the problem in my own way.
The Budget-Mr. Poulin
We know that over 400,000 producers are interested in Canada's dairy industry and that over two million people are employed in that industry. We also know that butter is the most important product of that industry. City workers will readily understand that those two million people, who are in fact consumers, make up a very important market, since those same workers purchase manufactured goods.
They will surely understand that, in their own interest, they should not ignore the agricultural class. They cannot risk that those two million consumers interested in dairy production stop purchasing their products. I believe it is not an overstatement to say that the Canadian dairy industry now stands in jeopardy.
There are various reasons for this, some of them rather obvious. First, there is the high price currently offered farmers for beef cattle. Last summer, in rural districts, those of my constituency at any rate, I saw dealers go up and down the countryside every day offering to buy from the farmers not only their beef cattle but their dairy cattle as well. Farmers are naturally tempted to sell their dairy cattle since this stock fetches a high price. That is the first threat.
Of course, the farmer has to be cautious and avoid cutting down his dairy herd, for while it takes very little time to cut down, it takes very much more time to build it up again.	,
The second danger is somewhat like the first, because of the fact that our dairy cattle find a ready market south of the border. On March 19 last, in reply to a question in my name on the order paper, we were told1 that 47,000 of our dairy cattle had been exported to the United States in 1950. There lies another temptation for the farmer. He is likely to yield to that temptation because he is always offered a high price.
The third danger lies in the manufacture and sale of margarine in this country. I must say I am very happy that the Quebec government has banned the manufacture and sale of margarine. In my humble opinion, margarine is one of the greatest threats still facing the dairy industry.
We note that between 1949 and 1950 the production of margarine has gone up 27 per cent. Also that in the same period butter production has decreased 6 per cent.
As for the consumption of margarine, we see that in 1950 it was up 30 per cent over 1949 and that in the same period butter sales had gone up only 2-5 per cent.

The Budget-Mr. Poulin
Plainly there has been a rapid and constant rise in production and consumption of margarine.
On the other hand, we find that butter production has fallen off while consumption remained at about the same level. Of course, I am no economist, but I have some business experience and it seems to me that these figures show clearly that margarine now endangers our butter production and consequently our dairy industry.
While I am dealing with the butter situation may I be permitted to mention what happened in the last couple of months, when butter was selling at 75, 80, 85 and even 90 cents a pound in our small villages.
Although the producer had sold his product last fall at 57 or 58 cents a pound, it was stored for the winter and, two or three months later, it sold at huge profits. I am not in a position to say who is responsible for this condition but it surely is untenable. It should not exist and should not be allowed to recur if it can be avoided. I know that some people are dissatisfied in my district and I fear that the public will be resentful, through no fault of their own.
I wish to add a few words about taxes, especially the general sales tax which has gone up 25 per cent. It has been said many times that this tax directly affects the consumer and will surely entail a higher cost of living. As another result-it can already be foreseen and all the newspapers have foretold it-the labour unions will request higher wages. What will happen? The increases will either be granted or they will not. If they are granted, they will have a direct effect on the cost of living, which will rise still more. If the salaries are not increased, well, a state of uneasiness will prevail amongst the working classes, an uneasiness which may well become dangerous.
The second tax levied-and it is perhaps more striking to the imagination-is the increase of 20 per cent in the income tax. Already this tax was imposed on a class of people with rather small incomes. I wish to express the opinion, if I may, that all incomes under $3,000 should not be taxed. Nevertheless the income tax is increased by 20 per cent. The poor will necessarily suffer, although taxpayers with large families have the benefit of certain exemptions based on the number of children, which is an excellent principle. It is generally acknowledged that this is all to the good. Nevertheless, in my opinion, the 20 per cent surtax is applied at too low a level of income and should have been applied to a much higher level.
There is perhaps one item that the government forgot to tax-and it was referred

to this evening rather ironically-and that is alcohol and beer. This omission has evoked many a pointed and caustic remark on the part of the public. But our country's treasurer simply forgot to levy a tax on liquor and beer. Yet it would have been easy since, in my opinion, they are not essential products. They may even be harmful in some instances. Revenue from taxes on liquor amounted in 1950 to $107 million. If the two taxes I have just mentioned, that is a 20 per cent tax and a 25 per cent tax, had been added to this, the tax would have stood at 45 per cent and the revenue would have been increased by some $50 million.
I know that there is a limit to increasing levies and that any product that is too heavily taxed might not sell so well or be consumed so widely and might not bring so much revenue. The country would be no worse off if the day ever came when no liquor at all was consumed. That would be no great evil. At this point, may I recall an incident that occurred in 1942 when we were then going through a very trying period. The world was waging a war that threatened to destroy everything. We needed all our strength. I well recall that on Christmas day 1942, the late prime minister, Mr. King, took the trouble to broadcast a plea to the nation. Pointing out that we needed all our energy for the defence effort, he asked the Canadian people to abstain entirely and to practise temperance.
If that was the right thing to do then, it would certainly be all the more so now. Once again, may I say that even if consumption of liquor were to disappear because of excessive taxation, that would not be such a great evil for the country.
For some time now, the government have been requested to control prices, to take steps in order to prevent too rapid increases in the price of foodstuffs. Reference was made to controls, to a controlled economy. It was stated that there was to be no interference with private enterprise. All that is all right. Personally, I am all for it. During the last war, controls were imposed and prices were frozen.
I am a believer in free enterprise just as long as it does not deprive a certain portion of the people of their liberty. I am anything but a socialist. Needless to say, I am no communist. I should not have to assert it, in spite of what has been said in this house by the member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Cannon), who claims I have been repeating communistic propaganda. He need not fear; I am not spreading any communistic propaganda at all.

The Budget-Mr. Poulin
However, it cannot be denied that today the poorer classes are in an absolutely miserable way. If we do not wish them to rise in revolt some day, we will have to seriously consider their plight.
I wonder if the situation is really well known, if we know exactly what goes on among our poorer people? I would like to be entirely impartial. I have no wish to criticize needlessly but I do think that most of our public men are not well acquainted with the true state of affairs, do not really know what goes on in our poorer families and that, consequently, they have not much to offer in the way of suggestions towards putting things right, in order to help out those of less than modest means.
May I be permitted to make a humble suggestion. I have no illusions on that point for I know perfectly well that it will not be well received. Besides, no one is bound to accept it. To remedy the state of poverty in which a large part of our people find themselves due to the high cost of living, the government might double the rate of family allowances. I know that it would cost something like $275 million a year. It is a lot of money and it would mean new taxes. These taxes would have to be levied where they would not affect directly the poorer classes.
I was wondering a moment ago if the statesmen are really aware of the situation. Let us consider the cost of a few items taken from the list of consumer goods; milk, for example, which sells from 18 to 20 cents a quart. It costs between $5 and $6 a month to buy milk for one child, if we take for granted that a child should get a minimum of one quart of milk a day. A man having five children, infants or older children-. such families are not uncommon here-he will have to spend from $25 to $30 a month on that one item.
And now butter, which sells at 70 cents per pound. Let us say that a child needs trounces per day, which is not exaggerated. It will cost $2 per month per child, or $10 for the family. Thus for those items only, milk and butter, that family will have to spend between $35 and $40 a month.
To that must be added bread, meat, vegetables and a few sweets; all of which are essential to the normal development of children. If we add clothes, shoes, etc., how can the mother of a large family in the low-income bracket give her children the bare
necessities? That means privation for the children, anxiety for the parents and continuous nervous strain for everybody. Should such economic conditions persist, it is highly probable that such a family would bring up underdeveloped citizens both physically and intellectually, individuals unprepared to play their part, embittered, aroused and perhaps persecuted, of which at least a few will easily fall prey to subversive propaganda.
However true it may be, as the old saying goes, that society is no better than the family, it is one thing that is apparently overlooked in certain quarters. This is not merely an opinion but an established fact recognized by leading sociologists of all races and creeds. In seeking to make my humble contribution to this debate tonight, it is chiefly in order to champion the cause of the family, particularly the large family, the bulwark of society. I did suggest to the government a few moments ago to double the amount of family allowances as a means of protecting the family, and therefore society, in these troubled times.
Money can always be found though not always from the right source whenever preparations have to be made to prevent war. We rightly fear that an enemy from without might destroy our institutions, our freedom and our rights.
Let us not forget however that the enemy from within can achieve the same resiults, as surely if not as openly, by slowly undermining the very foundations of our society.
Let us give our taxation and economic policies a definite family trend; let us protect the family against too heavy taxes. Let us give it, on the other hand, the financial assistance it requires to carry on; let us spare the family the "undeserved misery" mentioned by a great pope.
When danger becomes more threatening, when a call is made for defenders of the country, where do we draw generously to ensure a continuous flow of soldiers? From the abundant source of large families.
The homeland sometimes asks from the mother the sacrifice of two, three and even four sons. It has happened during the two last wars. In return, at least, let the country be generous towards her, let the country support her in her arduous task, let the country give her all facilities in her work of salvation.
To provide for the security of our families is to provide for the security of society.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed1 a pleasure to avail

The Budget-Mr. Dube myself of this opportunity of saying a few words in this house to draw the attention of the government to certain necessary projects in my constituency of Restigouche-Madawaska.
I must say with regret, Mr. Speaker, that my constituency is not receiving its rightful share of money spent in this country.
The citizens of Campbellton derive their living almost exclusively from trade within the limits of their city. It is therefore most important that transportation facilities should be improved there. This requires, above all, the erection of a bridge across the Restigouche river. At present, the majority of the people have to purchase what they need by catalogue, as there is no means of crossing the river, especially in the spring and fall, when the ferry service is suspended. That situation hampers the city's development. The only remedy is to build a bridge.
You probably heard, Mr. Speaker, that the ferry which operated between Campbellton and Cross Point on the Restigouche river was destroyed by fire. Following this catastrophe, a delegation of businessmen from that district waited on the Quebec and Ottawa governments early in April in order to convince the appropriate authorities that a bridge over that river-we have been requesting it for more than thirty years-is essential to the inhabitants of both shores.
I do not hesitate to urge the government, once again, to undertake the building of this bridge which would improve the lot of these people and link Quebec and New Brunswick in a friendly manner. The city of Campbellton boasts modern hospitals, specialists in surgery, movie houses, arenas, garages, stores of every description and so on. It is also a valuable seaport, as well as the terminal point of an important railway. However, Campbellton's industrial development was delayed by the lack of permanent communications between the two provinces.
I am convinced that if the Department of Public Works took the trouble of making an investigation, based on the representations made by civic organizations such as the town council and the chamber of commerce, they would realize the necessity of carrying out this project for the greater benefit of the people in general.
For several months, indeed for several years, the municipal authorities have been


asking that a bridge be erected over the Restigouche river. The members of the committee in charge of this project had to overcome many obstacles, but they are prepared to sacrifice time and money to achieve their end, namely, the development of trade, the welfare of the farmers and the establishment of new industries.
From the political point of view, it would serve to strengthen the bonds which unite us with our northern neighbours, thus promoting national unity.
Looking at the matter from a personal point of view, we could then, when visiting Quebec, avoid a lot of inconveniences-for example, the annoyance of having to wait for the ferry, to name but one.
Allow me, Mr Speaker, to recall that we have repeatedly requested the C.N.R. authorities to erect a freight shed in the town of Edmundston. We consider this to be a very necessary project since the town has a fairly important railway terminal. I want to add that revenues from the storing of freight, for the year 1950, reached a figure of over two million dollars. According to information received from authorized sources, $50,000 has been voted for the construction of that shed. The structure we have now was built back in 1914 when the town had a population of only two or three thousand. Now the population is 10,000. Trade has grown threefold since those days. I am proud to say we are the only division in the Atlantic region to show a profit. Yet it is the division that receives the least encouragement.
Moreover our station, which was built at the same time as the shed, is in a very bad condition. It has no waiting-room, and travellers should be provided with the comfort they deserve for patronizing the Canadian National Railways.
I therefore urge the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) to speed up the building of a shed and station at that point.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that I would fail in my duty if I did not also mention the plight of the potato-growers of my constituency in the past few years. The government has put a ceiling price on their product. Had it not been for the set price they could have sold their potatoes at $5 or $6 a barrel, and they would all be better off today.
I am disappointed to learn that no answer has been given to the delegation which came

to Ottawa, during the week of March 20, to meet officials of the Department of Agriculture and ask the government to include their product in the list of subsidized commodities. If the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) persists in his refusal to grant them the help they ask for, many of them will have to give up their farms. This would be unfortunate after all the sacrifices the farmers have made in order to improve their crops.
I am counting on the good will of the Minister of Agriculture and I hope he will
The Budget-Mr. Dube reconsider his decision and help this group of citizens so worthy of all his consideration.
